extraction.body: A giant data center is making engineers throw out the rule book The undying thirst for smarter (historically, that means larger) AI models and greater adoption of the ones we already have has led to an explosion in data-center construction projects , unparalleled both in number and scale. Chief among them is Meta’s planned 5-gigawatt data center in Louisiana, called Hyperion, announced in June of 2025. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Hyperion will “cover a significant part of the footprint of Manhattan,” and the first phase—a 2-GW version—will be completed by 2030. Though the project’s stated 5-GW scale is the largest among its peers, it’s just one of several dozen similar projects now underway. According to Michael Guckes, chief economist at construction-software company ConstructConnect , spending on data centers topped US $27 billion by July of 2025 and, once the full-year figures are tallied, will easily exceed $60 billion. Hyperion alone accounts for about a quarter of that. For the engineers assigned to bring these projects to life, the mix of challenges involved represent a unique moment. The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago. At the same time, the breakneck pace of building comes paired with serious problems. Modern data-center construction frequently requires an influx of temporary workers and sharply increases noise, traffic, pollution, and often local electricity prices. And the environmental toll remains a concern long after facilities are built due to the unprecedented 24/7 energy demands of AI data centers which, according to one recent study, could emit the equivalent of tens of millions of tonnes of CO 2 annually in the United States alone. Regardless of these issues, large AI companies, and the engineers they hire, are going full steam ahead on giant data-center construction. So, what does it really take to build an unprecedentedly large data center? The stereotypical data-center building rests on a reinforced concrete slab foundation. That’s paired with a steel skeleton and poured concrete wall panels. The finished building is called a “shell,” a term that implies the structure itself is a secondary concern. Meta has even used gigantic tents to throw up temporary data centers. Still, the scale of the largest AI data centers brings unique challenges. “The biggest challenge is often what’s under the surface. Unstable, corrosive, or expansive soils can lead to delays and require serious intervention,” says Robert Haley , vice president at construction consulting firm Jacobs . Amanda Carter , a senior technical lead at Stantec , said a soil’s thermal conductivity is also important, as most electrical infrastructure is placed underground. “If the soil has high thermal resistivity, it’s going to be difficult to dissipate [heat].” Engineers may take hundreds or thousands of soil samples before construction can begin. GPUs Modern AI data centers often use rack-scale systems, such as the Nvidia GB200 NVL72, which occupy a single data-center rack. Each rack contains 72 GPUs , 36 CPUs, and up to 13.4 terabytes of GPU memory. The racks measure over 2.2 meters tall and weigh over one and a half tonnes, forcing AI data centers to use thicker concrete with more reinforcement to bear the load. A single GB200 rack can use up to 120 kilowatts. If Hyperion meets its 5-gigawatt goals, the data-center campus could include over 41,000 rack-scale systems, for a total of more than 3 million GPUs. The final number of GPUs used by Hyperion is likely to be less than that, though only because future GPUs will be larger, more capable, and use more power. According to ConstructConnect, spending on data centers neared US $27 billion through July of 2025 and, according to the latest data, will tally close to $60 billion through the end of the year. Meta’s Hyperion project is a big slice of the pie, at $10 billion. Data-center spending has become an important prop for the construction industry, which is seeing reduced demand in other areas, such as residential construction and public infrastructure. ConstructConnect’s third quarter 2025 financial report stated that the quarter’s decline “would have been far more severe without an $11 billion surge in data center starts.” There’s apparently no shortage of eligible sites, however, as both the number of data centers under construction, and the money spent on them, has skyrocketed. The spending has allowed companies building data centers to throw out the rule book. Prior to the AI boom, most data centers relied on tried-and-true designs that prioritized inexpensive and efficient construction. Big tech’s willingness to spend has shifted the focus to speed and scale. Meta’s Richland Parish site also highlights a problem that’s priority No. 1 for both AI data centers and their critics: power. Data centers have always drawn large amounts of power, which nudged data-center construction to cluster in hubs where local utilities were responsive to their demands. Virginia’s electric utility, Dominion Energy, met demand with agreements to build new infrastructure, often with a focus on renewable energy . The power demands of the largest AI data centers, though, have caught even the most responsive utilities off guard. A report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory , in California, estimated the entire U.S. data-center industry consumed an average load of roughly 8 GW of power in 2014 . Today, the largest AI data-center campuses are built to handle up to a gigawatt each, and Meta’s Hyperion is projected to require 5 GW. “Data centers are exasperating issues for a lot of utilities,” says Abbe Ramanan , project director at the Clean Energy Group, a Vermont-based nonprofit. Entergy frames the new plants as a win for the state. “A core pillar of Entergy and Meta’s agreement is that Meta pays for the full cost of the utility infrastructure,” says Daniel Kline , director of power-delivery planning and policy at Entergy. The utility expects that “customer bills will be lower than they otherwise would have been.” That would prove an exception, as a recent report from Bloomberg found electricity rates in regions with data centers are more likely to increase than in regions without. Research published in Nature in 2025 projects that data-center emissions will range from 24 million to 44 million CO2-equivalent metric tonnes annually through 2030 in the United States alone. While some materials used in data centers, such as concrete, lead to significant emissions, the majority of these emissions will result from the high energy demands of AI servers . Estimating the carbon emissions of Hyperion is difficult, as the project won’t be completed until 2030. Assuming that the three new natural gas plants that are planned for construction as part of the project produce emissions typical for their type, however, the plants could lead to full life-cycle emissions of between 4 million and 10 million metric tons of CO2 annually—roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of a country like Latvia . Data centers are typically built from concrete, with steel used as a skeleton to reinforce and shape the concrete shell. While the foundation is often poured concrete, the walls and floors are most often built from prefabricated concrete panels that can span up to 23 meters. Floors use a reinforced T-shape, similar to a steel girder, measuring up to 1.2 meters across at its thickest point. The largest data centers include hundreds of these concrete panels. The America Cement Association projects that the current surge in building will require 1 million tonnes of cement over the next three years , though that’s still a tiny fraction of the overall cement industry, which weighed in at roughly 103 million tonnes in 2024 . The plants, which will generate a combined 2.26 GW, will use combined-cycle gas turbines that recapture waste heat from exhaust. This boosts thermal efficiency to 60 percent and beyond, meaning more fuel is converted to useful energy. Simple-cycle turbines, by contrast, vent the exhaust, which lowers efficiency to around 40 percent. Even so, total life-cycle emissions for the Hyperion plants could range from 4 million to over 10 million tonnes of CO2 each year, depending on how frequently the plants are put in use and the final efficiency benchmarks once built. On the high end, that’s as much CO2 as produced by over 2 million passenger cars. Fortunately, not all of Meta’s data centers take the same approach to power. The undying thirst for smarter (historically, that means larger) AI models and greater adoption of the ones we already have has led to an explosion in data-center construction projects , unparalleled both in number and scale. Chief among them is Meta’s planned 5-gigawatt data center in Louisiana, called Hyperion, announced in June of 2025. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Hyperion will “cover a significant part of the footprint of Manhattan,” and the first phase—a 2-GW version—will be completed by 2030.

Though the project’s stated 5-GW scale is the largest among its peers, it’s just one of several dozen similar projects now underway. According to Michael Guckes, chief economist at construction-software company ConstructConnect , spending on data centers topped US $27 billion by July of 2025 and, once the full-year figures are tallied, will easily exceed $60 billion. Hyperion alone accounts for about a quarter of that.

For the engineers assigned to bring these projects to life, the mix of challenges involved represent a unique moment. The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago.

At the same time, the breakneck pace of building comes paired with serious problems. Modern data-center construction frequently requires an influx of temporary workers and sharply increases noise, traffic, pollution, and often local electricity prices. And the environmental toll remains a concern long after facilities are built due to the unprecedented 24/7 energy demands of AI data centers which, according to one recent study, could emit the equivalent of tens of millions of tonnes of CO 2 annually in the United States alone.

Regardless of these issues, large AI companies, and the engineers they hire, are going full steam ahead on giant data-center construction. So, what does it really take to build an unprecedentedly large data center?

The stereotypical data-center building rests on a reinforced concrete slab foundation. That’s paired with a steel skeleton and poured concrete wall panels. The finished building is called a “shell,” a term that implies the structure itself is a secondary concern. Meta has even used gigantic tents to throw up temporary data centers.

Still, the scale of the largest AI data centers brings unique challenges. “The biggest challenge is often what’s under the surface. Unstable, corrosive, or expansive soils can lead to delays and require serious intervention,” says Robert Haley , vice president at construction consulting firm Jacobs . Amanda Carter , a senior technical lead at Stantec , said a soil’s thermal conductivity is also important, as most electrical infrastructure is placed underground. “If the soil has high thermal resistivity, it’s going to be difficult to dissipate [heat].” Engineers may take hundreds or thousands of soil samples before construction can begin.

GPUs Modern AI data centers often use rack-scale systems, such as the Nvidia GB200 NVL72, which occupy a single data-center rack. Each rack contains 72 GPUs , 36 CPUs, and up to 13.4 terabytes of GPU memory. The racks measure over 2.2 meters tall and weigh over one and a half tonnes, forcing AI data centers to use thicker concrete with more reinforcement to bear the load.

A single GB200 rack can use up to 120 kilowatts. If Hyperion meets its 5-gigawatt goals, the data-center campus could include over 41,000 rack-scale systems, for a total of more than 3 million GPUs. The final number of GPUs used by Hyperion is likely to be less than that, though only because future GPUs will be larger, more capable, and use more power.

According to ConstructConnect, spending on data centers neared US $27 billion through July of 2025 and, according to the latest data, will tally close to $60 billion through the end of the year. Meta’s Hyperion project is a big slice of the pie, at $10 billion.

ConstructConnect’s third quarter 2025 financial report stated that the quarter’s decline “would have been far more severe without an $11 billion surge in data center starts.”

There’s apparently no shortage of eligible sites, however, as both the number of data centers under construction, and the money spent on them, has skyrocketed. The spending has allowed companies building data centers to throw out the rule book. Prior to the AI boom, most data centers relied on tried-and-true designs that prioritized inexpensive and efficient construction. Big tech’s willingness to spend has shifted the focus to speed and scale.

extraction.body: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The push against data centers has been well-documented. One independent tracker counts nearly 150 data center moratoriums in place all across the state. Opponents are concerned about a wide variety of issues, including the impact the centers have on the environment and their utility bills. At the same time, supporters point to the fact that those data centers are bringing billions of dollars in investment and new opportunities for construction workers. As data centers continue to expand across Ohio, so does the demand for the workers needed to build them. “We’ve got in-house architecture and engineering, licensed and stamped in all 50 states,” said Will Goodin, vice president of project development for Terrapin Construction Group. Terrapin Construction Group designs data centers across the country with four separate projects currently in Ohio. “And that’s inclusive of mechanical, electrical, plumbing as well as engineering, civil, so site work and structural work as well,” Goodin said. He said the growing number of data center projects is creating more business for his company, making over $100 million from design, construction and procurement of HVAC equipment this year, and they’re on track to triple that next year. “We’ve seen a huge uptick in not only design but also a lot of pre-construction, a lot of construction specifically in the data center asset class,” Goodin said. Goodin said demand for the specialized equipment needed to build these facilities is also high, with some supplies taking months to arrive. “There’s huge lead times depending on the types of equipment that you’re looking to source for your project. Anywhere from 18- to 50-plus weeks for any number of transfer switches, switch gears, chillers, things of that nature,” Goodin said. That demand creates opportunities for a wide range of skilled trades, including electricians, mechanical contractors, framers and carpenters. Goodin said the steady pipeline of projects is providing job security for his company and the subcontractors it relies on. But he recognizes the industry is not without controversy. “Depending on who you ask, it’s kind of a loaded, complicated issue but we’re very excited to be a resource for folks who are looking to get into this business and are expanding their current operations,” Goodin said. Across Ohio, communities are pushing back against data center development. As more communities consider putting development on pause, the question becomes: How many jobs do these facilities actually create once construction is over? Case Western Reserve University Economics Professor Jonathan Ernest said the initial construction phase can provide a significant employment boost. “There are fewer people onsite for the longterm with lots of jobs in an area. So we’re not likely to get entire cities that are built around the one plant that everyone works at we’re not likely to get that with data centers because they don’t need that many capacity of people on site for the long run,” said Ernest. So, while the construction boom is creating opportunities for Ohio’s skilled trades, Ernest said communities should take a closer look at what those projects will mean for the local workforce once the facilities are up and running. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, there are 26 data centers currently being constructed, with another 54 in the planning phase.

coreStoryFacts.text: While anxiety around AI replacing white-collar jobs has reached a fever pitch , the data center boom is creating lucrative opportunities for skilled trade workers.

Specialized and technical professionals moving into high-level data center roles often see a 25% to 30% pay increase, according to staffing firm Kelly Services, which shared estimates with CNBC based on internal and third-party data.
It said the premium can vary by role and full-spectrum salary data is still emerging for data center positions.

Amazon said last month that it's committing $12 billion to build a new AI data center in Louisiana, which will create 540 full-time jobs on site as well as 1,700 other roles for electricians, technicians, and security specialists.

A key factor driving these salaries higher is a shortage of trade workers , with the U.S. facing a potential shortfall of 1.9 million manufacturing workers by 2033, according to 2025 data from the National Association of Manufacturers.
"The digital revolution requires a massive physical foundation," Sander van't Noordende, CEO of the world's largest recruitment firm Randstad , told CNBC.

Earlier in March, BlackRock launched a $100 million initiative to empower the next generation of trades workers, as CEO Larry Fink stressed that capital alone is not enough to realize the $10 trillion of investment needed for infrastructure.
Meanwhile, job listings for traditional skilled trade jobs such as construction workers and electricians increased by 27%, according to Randstad's analysis.
But the boom in demand for key AI infrastructure jobs also faces several hurdles, including an aging demographic and geographical constraints.
A rural Texas county on Tuesday approved a one-year pause on the construction of new data centers in unincorporated areas, citing public safety and public health concerns.
The decision comes amid a growing statewide battle over Texas’ data center boom, particularly in rural counties where projects are rapidly moving into unincorporated areas with no zoning.
In neighboring counties, residents have increasingly voiced frustration that projects are advancing faster than public understanding or oversight.

“The data center folks have found a sweet spot in the state that has limited regulations, limited enforcement, limited code, and they’re coming faster than we can keep up with,” said Hill County Commissioner Jim Holcomb.
Representatives of data center developers pleaded with the county to reject the moratorium and said they are bringing money to the county for schools and roads.
Other Texas counties, including Hood and Hays counties, have explored similar moratoriums.
Brassel said the court still felt a responsibility to put guardrails in place during what he called a “land rush” — even if it meant being the first county to test the limits of Texas law.
He said he has talked to many county judges and they were waiting for someone to take this step first.
County Judge Shane Brassell said the temporary pause will allow officials time to study the effects of data centers before projects move forward.
It’s not clear how many data centers have been proposed for Hill County.

Paul Bettencourt sent a letter to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton on the day of the Hood County vote, claiming that counties have no constitutional or statutory authority to impose development moratoriums and asking Paxton to investigate counties that passed one.
Hood County commissioners rejected the pause.

The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago.

extraction.body: Demand for new AI data centers is surging, but they can't build themselves. Big Tech is funneling billions into building out these specialized facilities , with the four hyperscalers, Alphabet , Microsoft , Meta , and Amazon , committing nearly $700 billion in combined capex spending this year to fund these developments. Amazon said last month that it's committing $12 billion to build a new AI data center in Louisiana, which will create 540 full-time jobs on site as well as 1,700 other roles for electricians, technicians, and security specialists. Meta also invested $27 billion last year in a joint venture with Blue Owl Capital to construct its mammoth Hyperion data center in Louisiana, which is expected to consume more electricity than the city of New Orleans. While anxiety around AI replacing white-collar jobs has reached a fever pitch , the data center boom is creating lucrative opportunities for skilled trade workers. "The digital revolution requires a massive physical foundation," Sander van't Noordende, CEO of the world's largest recruitment firm Randstad , told CNBC. "Ultimately, the real constraint on global tech growth isn't solely related to a shortage of microchips, energy, or capital; it is the severe scarcity of the specialized talent required to build it." Between 2022 and 2026, demand for robotic technicians increased by 107%, according to a global analysis of 50 million job postings released by Randstad on Wednesday. For cooling — or HVAC — system engineers, the growth rate was 67%, and vacancies for industrial automation technicians grew by 51%. Meanwhile, job listings for traditional skilled trade jobs such as construction workers and electricians increased by 27%, according to Randstad's analysis. "The debate around AI's impact on the labor market often focuses entirely on the software side, specifically, whether generative models will displace white-collar jobs. But a critical reality is being completely overlooked: AI cannot build its own data centers," Noordende said via emailed comments. With roughly 12,000 data centers existing globally today, and thousands more to be built to house high-performance AI computing capacity, it's essential to update outdated mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems every four to six years, according to Mike Mathews, digital infrastructure leader at professional services firm Marsh. Mathews noted "massive growth areas specific to labor" as a result of these retrofitting requirements, with network engineers, electricians, mechanical engineers, and plumbing and heating contractors deployed to install new liquid cooling systems. A fourth-generation plumber himself, Mathews described these roles as "new-collar" jobs, which will see traditional white-collar and blue-collar employees working alongside each other and being valued the same. "The data center space will be the first time when we've had highly compensated, high-skilled trades workers physically working next to network engineers who have college degrees. And I think it's a great social blend that we're going to have throughout data centers," Mathews added. Randstad's Noordende said that a "scarcity premium is taking effect" and that advertised wages for HVAC engineers have increased by roughly 10% to 15% in the past four years. "As AI infrastructure demand outpaces a shrinking labor supply, wage growth is rising significantly for these specialized roles," Noordende said, adding that six-figure salaries are achievable in the sector. Specialized and technical professionals moving into high-level data center roles often see a 25% to 30% pay increase, according to staffing firm Kelly Services, which shared estimates with CNBC based on internal and third-party data. It said the premium can vary by role and full-spectrum salary data is still emerging for data center positions. Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang – a central figure behind the AI data center boom – predicted in January that "six-figure salaries" are on the horizon for the workers building AI factories. A key factor driving these salaries higher is a shortage of trade workers , with the U.S. facing a potential shortfall of 1.9 million manufacturing workers by 2033, according to 2025 data from the National Association of Manufacturers. Meanwhile, the U.S.-based Associated Builders and Contractors trade group estimates that nearly half a million new workers will be needed in 2027, up from the 349,000 needed in 2026. "[The skills shortage is] a huge issue now, and it's only going to get worse," Gary Wojtaszek, executive chairman and interim CEO of Pure Data Centres, told CNBC. "The good thing is AI won't replace any of those jobs — someone needs to man those machines, so those are really important jobs, and that is a huge challenge for the industry overall." In order to overcome the skills shortage, businesses and governments will need to invest in training programs, Randstad's Noordende said. The skills shortage is also leading to cross-industry poaching as there's a lot of overlap in the operational technical skills needed for energy, defense, and tech, according to William Self, chief workforce strategist at global workforce consulting firm Mercer. Earlier in March, BlackRock launched a $100 million initiative to empower the next generation of trades workers, as CEO Larry Fink stressed that capital alone is not enough to realize the $10 trillion of investment needed for infrastructure. "[The] skills profile is evolving faster than traditional job descriptions can track," Mercer's Self said in a virtual press briefing on the topic. "Given the supply shortage, the companies that win this talent race will be the ones investing in both traditional recruiting and non-traditional workforce development. I'm seeing apprenticeship programs, community college partnerships, military veteran pipelines, and even internal talent academies to grow companies' own talent." But the boom in demand for key AI infrastructure jobs also faces several hurdles, including an aging demographic and geographical constraints. Roughly 1 in 4 workers globally is nearing retirement age, and the talent pool is not being replenished fast enough, according to Noordende. "Unlike software developers who can often work remotely, skilled trades possess very low geographic mobility," he said. "An equipment technician or construction worker must be physically on-site. When a company builds a new AI data center or manufacturing plant, it is a region-changing event that can instantly exhaust local talent pools. What will be challenging to predict going forward is how much of a "hazard pay rate" will be built into salaries in the future, Mercer's Self said.

passages: Regardless of these issues, large AI companies, and the engineers they hire, are going full steam ahead on giant data-center construction.
So, what does it really take to build an unprecedentedly large data center?

The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago.
Fortunately, not all of Meta’s data centers take the same approach to power.

Just one Hyperion data center built at the Richland Parish site will consume twice as much power as xAI’s Colossus which, at the time of its completion in the summer of 2024, was among the largest data centers yet built.
Data-center spending has become an important prop for the construction industry, which is seeing reduced demand in other areas, such as residential construction and public infrastructure.

The stereotypical data-center building rests on a reinforced concrete slab foundation.
There’s apparently no shortage of eligible sites, however, as both the number of data centers under construction, and the money spent on them, has skyrocketed.

Prior to the AI boom, most data centers relied on tried-and-true designs that prioritized inexpensive and efficient construction.

extraction.body: A giant data center is making engineers throw out the rule book The undying thirst for smarter (historically, that means larger) AI models and greater adoption of the ones we already have has led to an explosion in data-center construction projects , unparalleled both in number and scale. Chief among them is Meta’s planned 5-gigawatt data center in Louisiana, called Hyperion, announced in June of 2025. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Hyperion will “cover a significant part of the footprint of Manhattan,” and the first phase—a 2-GW version—will be completed by 2030. Though the project’s stated 5-GW scale is the largest among its peers, it’s just one of several dozen similar projects now underway. According to Michael Guckes, chief economist at construction-software company ConstructConnect , spending on data centers topped US $27 billion by July of 2025 and, once the full-year figures are tallied, will easily exceed $60 billion. Hyperion alone accounts for about a quarter of that. For the engineers assigned to bring these projects to life, the mix of challenges involved represent a unique moment. The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago. At the same time, the breakneck pace of building comes paired with serious problems. Modern data-center construction frequently requires an influx of temporary workers and sharply increases noise, traffic, pollution, and often local electricity prices. And the environmental toll remains a concern long after facilities are built due to the unprecedented 24/7 energy demands of AI data centers which, according to one recent study, could emit the equivalent of tens of millions of tonnes of CO 2 annually in the United States alone. Regardless of these issues, large AI companies, and the engineers they hire, are going full steam ahead on giant data-center construction. So, what does it really take to build an unprecedentedly large data center? The stereotypical data-center building rests on a reinforced concrete slab foundation. That’s paired with a steel skeleton and poured concrete wall panels. The finished building is called a “shell,” a term that implies the structure itself is a secondary concern. Meta has even used gigantic tents to throw up temporary data centers. Still, the scale of the largest AI data centers brings unique challenges. “The biggest challenge is often what’s under the surface. Unstable, corrosive, or expansive soils can lead to delays and require serious intervention,” says Robert Haley , vice president at construction consulting firm Jacobs . Amanda Carter , a senior technical lead at Stantec , said a soil’s thermal conductivity is also important, as most electrical infrastructure is placed underground. “If the soil has high thermal resistivity, it’s going to be difficult to dissipate [heat].” Engineers may take hundreds or thousands of soil samples before construction can begin. GPUs Modern AI data centers often use rack-scale systems, such as the Nvidia GB200 NVL72, which occupy a single data-center rack. Each rack contains 72 GPUs , 36 CPUs, and up to 13.4 terabytes of GPU memory. The racks measure over 2.2 meters tall and weigh over one and a half tonnes, forcing AI data centers to use thicker concrete with more reinforcement to bear the load. A single GB200 rack can use up to 120 kilowatts. If Hyperion meets its 5-gigawatt goals, the data-center campus could include over 41,000 rack-scale systems, for a total of more than 3 million GPUs. The final number of GPUs used by Hyperion is likely to be less than that, though only because future GPUs will be larger, more capable, and use more power. According to ConstructConnect, spending on data centers neared US $27 billion through July of 2025 and, according to the latest data, will tally close to $60 billion through the end of the year. Meta’s Hyperion project is a big slice of the pie, at $10 billion. Data-center spending has become an important prop for the construction industry, which is seeing reduced demand in other areas, such as residential construction and public infrastructure. ConstructConnect’s third quarter 2025 financial report stated that the quarter’s decline “would have been far more severe without an $11 billion surge in data center starts.” There’s apparently no shortage of eligible sites, however, as both the number of data centers under construction, and the money spent on them, has skyrocketed. The spending has allowed companies building data centers to throw out the rule book. Prior to the AI boom, most data centers relied on tried-and-true designs that prioritized inexpensive and efficient construction. Big tech’s willingness to spend has shifted the focus to speed and scale. Meta’s Richland Parish site also highlights a problem that’s priority No. 1 for both AI data centers and their critics: power. Data centers have always drawn large amounts of power, which nudged data-center construction to cluster in hubs where local utilities were responsive to their demands. Virginia’s electric utility, Dominion Energy, met demand with agreements to build new infrastructure, often with a focus on renewable energy . The power demands of the largest AI data centers, though, have caught even the most responsive utilities off guard. A report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory , in California, estimated the entire U.S. data-center industry consumed an average load of roughly 8 GW of power in 2014 . Today, the largest AI data-center campuses are built to handle up to a gigawatt each, and Meta’s Hyperion is projected to require 5 GW. “Data centers are exasperating issues for a lot of utilities,” says Abbe Ramanan , project director at the Clean Energy Group, a Vermont-based nonprofit. Entergy frames the new plants as a win for the state. “A core pillar of Entergy and Meta’s agreement is that Meta pays for the full cost of the utility infrastructure,” says Daniel Kline , director of power-delivery planning and policy at Entergy. The utility expects that “customer bills will be lower than they otherwise would have been.” That would prove an exception, as a recent report from Bloomberg found electricity rates in regions with data centers are more likely to increase than in regions without. Research published in Nature in 2025 projects that data-center emissions will range from 24 million to 44 million CO2-equivalent metric tonnes annually through 2030 in the United States alone. While some materials used in data centers, such as concrete, lead to significant emissions, the majority of these emissions will result from the high energy demands of AI servers . Estimating the carbon emissions of Hyperion is difficult, as the project won’t be completed until 2030. Assuming that the three new natural gas plants that are planned for construction as part of the project produce emissions typical for their type, however, the plants could lead to full life-cycle emissions of between 4 million and 10 million metric tons of CO2 annually—roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of a country like Latvia . Data centers are typically built from concrete, with steel used as a skeleton to reinforce and shape the concrete shell. While the foundation is often poured concrete, the walls and floors are most often built from prefabricated concrete panels that can span up to 23 meters. Floors use a reinforced T-shape, similar to a steel girder, measuring up to 1.2 meters across at its thickest point. The largest data centers include hundreds of these concrete panels. The America Cement Association projects that the current surge in building will require 1 million tonnes of cement over the next three years , though that’s still a tiny fraction of the overall cement industry, which weighed in at roughly 103 million tonnes in 2024 . The plants, which will generate a combined 2.26 GW, will use combined-cycle gas turbines that recapture waste heat from exhaust. This boosts thermal efficiency to 60 percent and beyond, meaning more fuel is converted to useful energy. Simple-cycle turbines, by contrast, vent the exhaust, which lowers efficiency to around 40 percent. Even so, total life-cycle emissions for the Hyperion plants could range from 4 million to over 10 million tonnes of CO2 each year, depending on how frequently the plants are put in use and the final efficiency benchmarks once built. On the high end, that’s as much CO2 as produced by over 2 million passenger cars. Fortunately, not all of Meta’s data centers take the same approach to power. The company has announced a plan to power Prometheus, a large data-center project in Ohio scheduled to come online before the end of 2026, with nuclear energy . But other big tech companies, spurred by the need to build data centers quickly, are taking a less efficient approach. xAI’s Colossus 2, located in Memphis, is the most extreme example. The company trucked dozens of temporary gas-turbine generators to power the site located in a suburban neighborhood. OpenAI , meanwhile, has gas turbines capable of generating up to 300 megawatts at its new Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas , slated to open later in 2026. Both use simple-cycle turbines with a much lower efficiency rating than the combined-cycle plants Entergy will build to power Hyperion. Demand for gas turbines is so intense, in fact, that wait times for new turbines are up to seven years . Some data centers are turning toward refurbished jet engines to obtain the turbines they need. Hyperion is expected to use 5 gigawatts of power across 11 buildings, which works out to just under 500 megawatts per building, assuming each will be similar to its siblings. That’s enough to power roughly 4.2 million U.S. homes. Just one Hyperion data center built at the Richland Parish site will consume twice as much power as xAI’s Colossus which, at the time of its completion in the summer of 2024, was among the largest data centers yet built. Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 —a rack-scale system—is currently a leading choice for AI data centers. A single GB200 rack contains 72 GPUs, 36 CPUs, and up to 17 terabytes of memory. It measures 2.2 meters tall, tips the scales at up to 1,553 kilograms, and consumes about 120 kilowatts—as much as around 100 U.S. homes. And this, according to Nvidia, is just the beginning. The company anticipates future racks could consume up to a megawatt each . The new power demands from rack-scale systems have consequences that are reflected in the design of the data center—even its footprint. In 2022 Meta broke ground on a new data center at a campus in Temple, Texas. According to SemiAnalysis , which studies AI data centers, construction began with the intent to build the data center in an H-shaped configuration common to other Meta data centers . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the buzz around Hyperion by saying it would cover a large chunk of Manhattan. Many took that to mean Hyperion would be a single building of that size, which isn’t correct. Hyperion will actually be a cluster of data centers—11 are currently planned—with over 370,000 square meters of floor space. That’s a lot smaller even than New York City’s Central Park, which covers 6 percent of Manhattan. Meta has room to grow, however. The Richland Parish site spans 14.7 million square meters in total, which is about a quarter the area of Manhattan. And the 370,000 square meters of floor space Hyperion is expected to provide doesn’t include external infrastructure, such as the three new combined-cycle gas power plants Louisiana utility Entergy is building to power the project. Construction was paused midway in December of 2022, however, as part of a company-wide review of its data-center infrastructure . Meta decided to knock down the structure it had built and start from scratch. The reasons for this decision were never made public, but analysts believe it was due to the old design’s inability to deliver sufficient electricity to new, power-hungry AI racks. Construction resumed in 2023. Meta’s replacement ditches the H-shaped building for simple, long, rectangular structures, each flanked by rows of gas-turbine generators. While Meta’s plans are subject to change, Hyperion is currently expected to comprise 11 rectangular data centers, each packed with hundreds of thousands of GPUs, spread across the 13.6-square-kilometer Richland Parish campus.

Demand for gas turbines is so intense, in fact, that wait times for new turbines are up to seven years . Some data centers are turning toward refurbished jet engines to obtain the turbines they need.

Hyperion is expected to use 5 gigawatts of power across 11 buildings, which works out to just under 500 megawatts per building, assuming each will be similar to its siblings. That’s enough to power roughly 4.2 million U.S. homes.

Just one Hyperion data center built at the Richland Parish site will consume twice as much power as xAI’s Colossus which, at the time of its completion in the summer of 2024, was among the largest data centers yet built.

Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 —a rack-scale system—is currently a leading choice for AI data centers. A single GB200 rack contains 72 GPUs, 36 CPUs, and up to 17 terabytes of memory. It measures 2.2 meters tall, tips the scales at up to 1,553 kilograms, and consumes about 120 kilowatts—as much as around 100 U.S. homes. And this, according to Nvidia, is just the beginning. The company anticipates future racks could consume up to a megawatt each .
The new power demands from rack-scale systems have consequences that are reflected in the design of the data center—even its footprint.

In 2022 Meta broke ground on a new data center at a campus in Temple, Texas. According to SemiAnalysis , which studies AI data centers, construction began with the intent to build the data center in an H-shaped configuration common to other Meta data centers .

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the buzz around Hyperion by saying it would cover a large chunk of Manhattan. Many took that to mean Hyperion would be a single building of that size, which isn’t correct. Hyperion will actually be a cluster of data centers—11 are currently planned—with over 370,000 square meters of floor space. That’s a lot smaller even than New York City’s Central Park, which covers 6 percent of Manhattan.

Meta has room to grow, however. The Richland Parish site spans 14.7 million square meters in total, which is about a quarter the area of Manhattan. And the 370,000 square meters of floor space Hyperion is expected to provide doesn’t include external infrastructure, such as the three new combined-cycle gas power plants Louisiana utility Entergy is building to power the project.

Construction was paused midway in December of 2022, however, as part of a company-wide review of its data-center infrastructure . Meta decided to knock down the structure it had built and start from scratch. The reasons for this decision were never made public, but analysts believe it was due to the old design’s inability to deliver sufficient electricity to new, power-hungry AI racks. Construction resumed in 2023.

Meta’s replacement ditches the H-shaped building for simple, long, rectangular structures, each flanked by rows of gas-turbine generators. While Meta’s plans are subject to change, Hyperion is currently expected to comprise 11 rectangular data centers, each packed with hundreds of thousands of GPUs, spread across the 13.6-square-kilometer Richland Parish campus.

relevantPassages.text: Regardless of these issues, large AI companies, and the engineers they hire, are going full steam ahead on giant data-center construction.
So, what does it really take to build an unprecedentedly large data center?

The world’s largest tech companies are opening their wallets to pay for new innovations in compute, cooling, and network technology designed to operate at a scale that would’ve seemed absurd five years ago.
Fortunately, not all of Meta’s data centers take the same approach to power.

Just one Hyperion data center built at the Richland Parish site will consume twice as much power as xAI’s Colossus which, at the time of its completion in the summer of 2024, was among the largest data centers yet built.
Data-center spending has become an important prop for the construction industry, which is seeing reduced demand in other areas, such as residential construction and public infrastructure.

According to Michael Guckes, chief economist at construction-software company ConstructConnect , spending on data centers topped US $27 billion by July of 2025 and, once the full-year figures are tallied, will easily exceed $60 billion.
But other big tech companies, spurred by the need to build data centers quickly, are taking a less efficient approach.
The stereotypical data-center building rests on a reinforced concrete slab foundation.
There’s apparently no shortage of eligible sites, however, as both the number of data centers under construction, and the money spent on them, has skyrocketed.
The spending has allowed companies building data centers to throw out the rule book.
Prior to the AI boom, most data centers relied on tried-and-true designs that prioritized inexpensive and efficient construction.

extraction.body: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The push against data centers has been well-documented. One independent tracker counts nearly 150 data center moratoriums in place all across the state. Opponents are concerned about a wide variety of issues, including the impact the centers have on the environment and their utility bills. At the same time, supporters point to the fact that those data centers are bringing billions of dollars in investment and new opportunities for construction workers. As data centers continue to expand across Ohio, so does the demand for the workers needed to build them. “We’ve got in-house architecture and engineering, licensed and stamped in all 50 states,” said Will Goodin, vice president of project development for Terrapin Construction Group. Terrapin Construction Group designs data centers across the country with four separate projects currently in Ohio. “And that’s inclusive of mechanical, electrical, plumbing as well as engineering, civil, so site work and structural work as well,” Goodin said. He said the growing number of data center projects is creating more business for his company, making over $100 million from design, construction and procurement of HVAC equipment this year, and they’re on track to triple that next year. “We’ve seen a huge uptick in not only design but also a lot of pre-construction, a lot of construction specifically in the data center asset class,” Goodin said. Goodin said demand for the specialized equipment needed to build these facilities is also high, with some supplies taking months to arrive. “There’s huge lead times depending on the types of equipment that you’re looking to source for your project. Anywhere from 18- to 50-plus weeks for any number of transfer switches, switch gears, chillers, things of that nature,” Goodin said. That demand creates opportunities for a wide range of skilled trades, including electricians, mechanical contractors, framers and carpenters. Goodin said the steady pipeline of projects is providing job security for his company and the subcontractors it relies on. But he recognizes the industry is not without controversy. “Depending on who you ask, it’s kind of a loaded, complicated issue but we’re very excited to be a resource for folks who are looking to get into this business and are expanding their current operations,” Goodin said. Across Ohio, communities are pushing back against data center development. As more communities consider putting development on pause, the question becomes: How many jobs do these facilities actually create once construction is over? Case Western Reserve University Economics Professor Jonathan Ernest said the initial construction phase can provide a significant employment boost. “There are fewer people onsite for the longterm with lots of jobs in an area. So we’re not likely to get entire cities that are built around the one plant that everyone works at we’re not likely to get that with data centers because they don’t need that many capacity of people on site for the long run,” said Ernest. So, while the construction boom is creating opportunities for Ohio’s skilled trades, Ernest said communities should take a closer look at what those projects will mean for the local workforce once the facilities are up and running. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, there are 26 data centers currently being constructed, with another 54 in the planning phase.

passages: A Chinese university with deep connections to the People's Liberation Army (PLA) purchased Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, according to procurement records.
The development highlights gaps in Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced technology.
This follows reports alleging that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The H200 is among Nvidia's most powerful processors for training and running advanced AI systems.
Its export is subject to US licensing requirements, which are generally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical University.
The contracts were valued at 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan.
They covered AI model fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning training.
The university also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
Shenzhen University purchased three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for 769,800 yuan in September.
Wuhan University of Technology purchased a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June.
The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted organisations and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy.
The university's management school purchased the processors from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.
Several of these institutions had close connections to China's defence industry or military research.
The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.
Restrictions were tightened in 2019, placing exports of controlled US technology to the institution under a policy of denial in most circumstances.
Several relatively unknown Chinese technology suppliers received the contracts.
However, the procurement records provided limited information about the processors' origins or the locations where the rented servers were operating.
Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers have the ability to fulfil orders before announcing successful bidders and signing contracts.
One announcement listed access to H800 processors at 10 yuan per chip-hour.
A separate procurement award published in January identified a supplier for six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a public institution based in Shenzhen.
Reuters had previously reported that Chinese institutions obtained restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers manufactured by Super Micro Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers.
Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 regarding his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.
US President Donald Trump's administration started permitting some H200 chip exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January.
Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 chips had reached China through indirect routes, even as Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.
Huang has maintained that continued US chip sales to China would help preserve America's technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on US technology.

This follows reports alleging that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has maintained that continued US chip sales to China would help preserve America's technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on US technology. However, lawmakers from both parties argue that access to Nvidia's most powerful AI processors could accelerate China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Democrats and Republicans in Congress have called for tighter controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, including chip-tracking requirements and increased congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 regarding his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University, one of China's elite defence-focused institutions belonging to the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group, purchased two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to a procurement record published on its website on October 21. The university's management school purchased the processors from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most powerful processors for training and running advanced AI systems. Its export is subject to US licensing requirements, which are generally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical University. The university also purchased access to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five computing-capacity rental contracts with Chinese companies this year, according to procurement records. Reuters was unable to determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. Restrictions were tightened in 2019, placing exports of controlled US technology to the institution under a policy of denial in most circumstances. A Chinese university with deep connections to the People's Liberation Army (PLA) purchased Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, according to procurement records. The development highlights gaps in Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced technology. The findings emerge as Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, face increasing scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying efforts to ease restrictions on chip sales to China. This follows reports alleging that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

Huang has maintained that continued US chip sales to China would help preserve America's technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on US technology. However, lawmakers from both parties argue that access to Nvidia's most powerful AI processors could accelerate China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.

Democrats and Republicans in Congress have called for tighter controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, including chip-tracking requirements and increased congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 regarding his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Northwestern Polytechnical University, one of China's elite defence-focused institutions belonging to the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group, purchased two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to a procurement record published on its website on October 21. The university's management school purchased the processors from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.

The H200 is among Nvidia's most powerful processors for training and running advanced AI systems. Its export is subject to US licensing requirements, which are generally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical University. The university also purchased access to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five computing-capacity rental contracts with Chinese companies this year, according to procurement records.

Reuters reported the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical University, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters was unable to determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.

Located in the northwestern Chinese city of Xi'an, Northwestern Polytechnical University conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. Restrictions were tightened in 2019, placing exports of controlled US technology to the institution under a policy of denial in most circumstances.

The university's purchases demonstrate how Chinese institutions with military connections continue to access US AI computing power through domestic suppliers. These arrangements include both direct chip purchases and rented access to servers equipped with the processors. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found that universities and research institutions had purchased US-restricted Nvidia chips or rented access to Nvidia-powered computing services through domestic suppliers. Several of these institutions had close connections to China's defence industry or military research.
Also Read: Anthropic's IPO could make its founders richer while leaving shareholders with limited control

US President Donald Trump's administration started permitting some H200 chip exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. However, the policy did not remove the separate restrictions imposed on organisations listed on the Entity List, including Northwestern Polytechnical University.

The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted organisations and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy. These requirements cover H200 processors and less advanced models. Besides purchasing two H200 chips outright for its management school, the university's procurement records show that its cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each.

The contracts were valued at 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan. They covered AI model fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning training. The university also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. Both A100 and A800 processors are prohibited from export to all Chinese entities, while the H200 is the most advanced processor mentioned in Northwestern Polytechnical University's procurement records.

In April, another institute at the university purchased computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips under a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. Several relatively unknown Chinese technology suppliers received the contracts. However, the procurement records provided limited information about the processors' origins or the locations where the rented servers were operating. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers have the ability to fulfil orders before announcing successful bidders and signing contracts.

The procurement records point to a broader market in which Chinese universities are obtaining restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services. Shenzhen University purchased three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology purchased a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June. It also bought four A100 chips in a separate transaction worth 344,000 yuan, according to the records.

Beihang University, another member of the Seven Sons of National Defense, purchased four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. The university has close connections to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements published in July and September identified suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips, which are restricted from export to China, to the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

One announcement listed access to H800 processors at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate procurement award published in January identified a supplier for six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a public institution based in Shenzhen. Reuters had previously reported that Chinese institutions obtained restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers manufactured by Super Micro Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers.

The news agency has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia processors sourced through overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 chips had reached China through indirect routes, even as Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.

Two government notices for the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences named suppliers of H800 and A800 computing services, one listing H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. The prices allow a direct comparison. Dividing the purchase price by two gives 437,350 yuan for a single H200, about $61,500 at the exchange rate implied by Reuters' own conversion. The seven-month rental of eight H200 chips cost 441,700 yuan, roughly the price of buying one chip outright, or about 7,900 yuan per chip per month. That comparison is calculated from the recorded prices and excludes hosting, power and support costs, which the records do not disclose. For a laboratory that needs computing power for a defined project, renting is the cheaper route, and it leaves no imported hardware for inspectors to trace. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced on 13 January that it would review licence applications for the Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X and similar chips case by case, provided security conditions were met. It estimated the volume rule could initially allow about 900,000 H200-equivalent chips. passages: Procurement records reviewed by Reuters show a blacklisted Chinese university bought two Nvidia H200 chips and rented more, exposing gaps in export controls.

A Chinese university on a United States export blacklist bought two of Nvidia's H200 artificial intelligence chips in October for 874,700 yuan, about $123,000, according to procurement records reviewed by Reuters.

Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an, one of China's "Seven Sons of National Defence" institutions, bought the chips for its management school from a domestic supplier, Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, rather than from Nvidia.

Reuters reported that the university also bought access to H200 and other restricted Nvidia processors this year through five contracts for rented computing capacity. Its cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, for servers containing eight H200 chips each.

Other records show rented servers with eight A100 and eight A800 chips, and an April contract worth 375,000 yuan requiring at least 24 A100 chips for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. Reuters reviewed 26 procurement and corporate records from this year.

The pattern reaches beyond one campus. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors for 769,800 yuan in September, and Beihang University, another defence-linked institution, bought four A800 chips for 489,000 yuan in April.

Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips separately for 344,000 yuan. Two government notices for the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences named suppliers of H800 and A800 computing services, one listing H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour.
The prices allow a direct comparison. Dividing the purchase price by two gives 437,350 yuan for a single H200, about $61,500 at the exchange rate implied by Reuters' own conversion.

The seven-month rental of eight H200 chips cost 441,700 yuan, roughly the price of buying one chip outright, or about 7,900 yuan per chip per month. That comparison is calculated from the recorded prices and excludes hosting, power and support costs, which the records do not disclose.
For a laboratory that needs computing power for a defined project, renting is the cheaper route, and it leaves no imported hardware for inspectors to trace.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced on 13 January that it would review licence applications for the Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X and similar chips case by case, provided security conditions were met.

Applicants must show exports will not reduce global production capacity available to US customers, that the Chinese buyer has export-compliance procedures including customer screening, and that the product has passed independent third-party testing in the United States.

The rule followed President Donald Trump's announcement of 8 December 2025. Under Secretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler said permitting H200 sales "under controlled conditions will strengthen the American technology ecosystem".

That change did not lift the separate Entity List restrictions on Northwestern Polytechnical, which Reuters reports was listed in 2001 over alleged missile-proliferation activity and military research, with a policy of denial applied from 2019.

Analysis published on 16 January by the AI policy research group IAPS argued the certifications are hard to verify and the security plans unenforceable once chips leave the United States. It estimated the volume rule could initially allow about 900,000 H200-equivalent chips.

The policy caps exports of a chip model to China at under half of cumulative sales of that model for end use in the United States, and requires lists of proposed remote-access customers. IAPS said there is no kill switch on an H200 and little leverage once the hardware is in China.
Domestic resale and rental sit beyond that reach. The records Reuters reviewed offered little information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operate.

Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment, and the universities named did not respond. No finding of an illegal export by Nvidia has been published, and the records do not establish one.

Reuters reported that Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged chip-tracking requirements and greater oversight of exports. Until then, procurement notices remain the clearest public evidence of what reaches blacklisted buyers.

The findings emerge as Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, face increasing scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying efforts to ease restrictions on chip sales to China. This follows reports alleging that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

Huang has maintained that continued US chip sales to China would help preserve America's technological leadership while keeping Chinese customers dependent on US technology. However, lawmakers from both parties argue that access to Nvidia's most powerful AI processors could accelerate China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.

Democrats and Republicans in Congress have called for tighter controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, including chip-tracking requirements and increased congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 regarding his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

The university's management school purchased the processors from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.

The H200 is among Nvidia's most powerful processors for training and running advanced AI systems. Its export is subject to US licensing requirements, which are generally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical University. The university also purchased access to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five computing-capacity rental contracts with Chinese companies this year, according to procurement records.

Reuters reported the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical University, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters was unable to determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.

Restrictions were tightened in 2019, placing exports of controlled US technology to the institution under a policy of denial in most circumstances.

The university's purchases demonstrate how Chinese institutions with military connections continue to access US AI computing power through domestic suppliers. passages: A first day of US-led talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi ended Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework between Ukraine , Russia and Europe and its top diplomat hailing "very productive" talks.

Ukraine has warned against a "Yalta 2.0", referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire.

Europe has been rattled as Trump has floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.

In a sign it is serious about reviving its demand to review Europe's decades-old security arrangement, Russia included a diplomat – Sergei Ryabkov – who logged Moscow's pre-invasion demand for NATO to pull back from eastern Europe.
"Allowing Russia to decide the borders of Europe will be a huge mistake," Denmark's Mette Frederiksen said, as she hosted Zelensky Tuesday.
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky described the talks as "constructive and quite substantive", adding that negotiators were working on a possible major exchange of prisoners.
Speaking in Copenhagen, the Ukrainian president also said it was "time" for Europe to choose a representative for the talks.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, United States and NATO reaffirmed their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO 's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part.
Russia, which occupies swathes of its smaller neighbour, pummelled Ukraine with more attacks overnight, cutting power to thousands as temperatures plummet.

sources.title: US calls for 'new' Europe security framework as Russia-Ukraine talks open
passages: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent's future.

As the talks opened, Kushner said the US hoped to "create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding" that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace".
Europe has been alarmed by Trump's plans and the EU said on the eve of the talks that "meaningful" security discussions can only take place after a ceasefire in Ukraine.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and NATO said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks.
Before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had demanded that NATO roll back troops from eastern Europe and has throughout the war aired its grievances towards the West.
"We hope that we will achieve a lasting peace for Ukraine," Umerov said, saying Kyiv wanted to discuss "security guarantees".
Ukraine has resisted Russia's invasion at a huge human cost, with thousands of civilians killed and millions forced to flee their homes.

extraction.body: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent's future. Kyiv's delegation -- headed by intelligence chief Rustem Umerov -- met the US envoys as well as European and NATO officials ahead of negotiations. Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands. As another winter of war approaches, Ukraine and its European allies fear Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat. Trump has also floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security. As the talks opened, Kushner said the US hoped to "create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding" that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace". He conceded there was a "lot of intense emotions" in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. Before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had demanded that NATO roll back troops from eastern Europe and has throughout the war aired its grievances towards the West. Russia has, for the first time, included in its delegation a diplomat -- Sergei Ryabkov -- who issued an ultimatum to the West on rewriting European security before Moscow launched the war. 'Merely one item' The head of Moscow's delegation, President Vladimir Putin's nationalistic aide Vladimir Medinsky, said he hoped Moscow's "bigger and more professional" team will "enable us to move forward on the path towards peace". A source in the Russian team earlier said that "the Ukrainian settlement, whilst a critically important issue, is merely one item on the agenda" of the talks. The main objective was "the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent", it added. NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks. In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and NATO said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture". Europe has been alarmed by Trump's plans and the EU said on the eve of the talks that "meaningful" security discussions can only take place after a ceasefire in Ukraine. Putin has refused broader ceasefires and face-to-face talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky, vowing his troops will press on to seize more land in Ukraine. 'Our people are waiting' Kyiv's top negotiator Umerov said Ukraine's priority in the talks remained securing a ceasefire. "Our people are waiting to end this war," he said. Ukraine has resisted Russia's invasion at a huge human cost, with thousands of civilians killed and millions forced to flee their homes. "We hope that we will achieve a lasting peace for Ukraine," Umerov said, saying Kyiv wanted to discuss "security guarantees". There is huge distrust in Ukraine towards Trump's aims, with the US leader appearing to veer towards Moscow this year, signing a diesel deal with Putin and criticising Zelensky. Trump hinted ahead of the talks that Ukraine might have to give up land, saying: "They're going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine." Russia occupies large swathes of Ukraine but, while its troops have inched westwards, they have not been able to seize the whole of the Donetsk region. Russia pummelled Ukraine in the run-up to the talks and carried out one of its deadliest strikes yet -- with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid. No 'particular expectations' Zelensky said the intensified strikes were part of Moscow's strategy of "putting pressure on Ukraine's position" at the negotiations. The Ukrainian military said on Tuesday that Russia had fired 162 drones and one ballistic missile overnight. Russia and Ukraine have held several rounds of failed talks during almost five years of war and hopes for peace are low. "We don't have any particular expectations," a senior Ukrainian official in Kyiv told AFP.
