passages: ABU DHABI: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Washington calling for a “new” security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent’s future.

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators sat facing each other, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff at the head of the table, in the first such talks since February in Geneva. Kushner said the US hoped to “create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding” that would secure “decades, if not centuries, of peace”.

The head of Moscow’s delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, said he hoped Moscow’s “bigger and more professional” team would “enable us to move forwards on the path towards peace”. A source in the Russian team said the Ukraine settlement was “merely one item on the agenda”, with the main objective “the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent”. The delegation includes, for the first time, diplomat Sergei Ryabkov, who issued Moscow’s ultimatum to the West on European security before the 2022 invasion.

Ukraine’s top negotiator Rustem Umerov said Kyiv’s priority remained securing a ceasefire and discussing security guarantees. “Our people are waiting to end this war,” he said. Before the talks, Ukraine’s delegation met the US envoys and European and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) officials, including NATO’s top commander in Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, who is also taking part. In a joint statement, they reaffirmed their “shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture”.

Europe has been alarmed by Trump’s plans, and the European Union (EU) said on the eve of the talks that “meaningful” security discussions could only take place after a ceasefire. Putin has refused broader ceasefires and face-to-face talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump hinted ahead of the talks that Ukraine might have to give up land, saying: “They’re going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine.” Russia occupies large parts of Ukraine but has not seized the whole of the Donetsk region, and demands that Kyiv surrender the areas it still holds there.

Russia pounded Ukraine in the run-up to the talks, with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid. The Ukrainian military said Russia fired 162 drones and one ballistic missile overnight into Tuesday. “We don’t have any particular expectations,” a senior Ukrainian official told AFP. — AFP

coreStoryFacts.text: A first day of US-led talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi ended Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework between Ukraine , Russia and Europe and its top diplomat hailing "very productive" talks.

Ukraine has warned against a "Yalta 2.0", referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire.

Europe has been rattled as Trump has floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.

In a sign it is serious about reviving its demand to review Europe's decades-old security arrangement, Russia included a diplomat – Sergei Ryabkov – who logged Moscow's pre-invasion demand for NATO to pull back from eastern Europe.
"Allowing Russia to decide the borders of Europe will be a huge mistake," Denmark's Mette Frederiksen said, as she hosted Zelensky Tuesday.
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky described the talks as "constructive and quite substantive", adding that negotiators were working on a possible major exchange of prisoners.
Speaking in Copenhagen, the Ukrainian president also said it was "time" for Europe to choose a representative for the talks.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, United States and NATO reaffirmed their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO 's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part.
Russia, which occupies swathes of its smaller neighbour, pummelled Ukraine with more attacks overnight, cutting power to thousands as temperatures plummet.

In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and NATO said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks.

sources.title: US calls for 'new' Europe security framework as Russia-Ukraine talks open
passages: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent's future.

As the talks opened, Kushner said the US hoped to "create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding" that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace".
Europe has been alarmed by Trump's plans and the EU said on the eve of the talks that "meaningful" security discussions can only take place after a ceasefire in Ukraine.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and NATO said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks.
Before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had demanded that NATO roll back troops from eastern Europe and has throughout the war aired its grievances towards the West.
"We hope that we will achieve a lasting peace for Ukraine," Umerov said, saying Kyiv wanted to discuss "security guarantees".
Ukraine has resisted Russia's invasion at a huge human cost, with thousands of civilians killed and millions forced to flee their homes.

extraction.body: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, with Washington calling for a "new" security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent's future. Kyiv's delegation -- headed by intelligence chief Rustem Umerov -- met the US envoys as well as European and NATO officials ahead of negotiations. Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands. As another winter of war approaches, Ukraine and its European allies fear Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat. Trump has also floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security. As the talks opened, Kushner said the US hoped to "create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding" that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace". He conceded there was a "lot of intense emotions" in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. Before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had demanded that NATO roll back troops from eastern Europe and has throughout the war aired its grievances towards the West. Russia has, for the first time, included in its delegation a diplomat -- Sergei Ryabkov -- who issued an ultimatum to the West on rewriting European security before Moscow launched the war. 'Merely one item' The head of Moscow's delegation, President Vladimir Putin's nationalistic aide Vladimir Medinsky, said he hoped Moscow's "bigger and more professional" team will "enable us to move forward on the path towards peace". A source in the Russian team earlier said that "the Ukrainian settlement, whilst a critically important issue, is merely one item on the agenda" of the talks. The main objective was "the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent", it added. NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks. In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and NATO said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture". Europe has been alarmed by Trump's plans and the EU said on the eve of the talks that "meaningful" security discussions can only take place after a ceasefire in Ukraine. Putin has refused broader ceasefires and face-to-face talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky, vowing his troops will press on to seize more land in Ukraine. 'Our people are waiting' Kyiv's top negotiator Umerov said Ukraine's priority in the talks remained securing a ceasefire. "Our people are waiting to end this war," he said. Ukraine has resisted Russia's invasion at a huge human cost, with thousands of civilians killed and millions forced to flee their homes. "We hope that we will achieve a lasting peace for Ukraine," Umerov said, saying Kyiv wanted to discuss "security guarantees". There is huge distrust in Ukraine towards Trump's aims, with the US leader appearing to veer towards Moscow this year, signing a diesel deal with Putin and criticising Zelensky. Trump hinted ahead of the talks that Ukraine might have to give up land, saying: "They're going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine." Russia occupies large swathes of Ukraine but, while its troops have inched westwards, they have not been able to seize the whole of the Donetsk region. Russia pummelled Ukraine in the run-up to the talks and carried out one of its deadliest strikes yet -- with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid. No 'particular expectations' Zelensky said the intensified strikes were part of Moscow's strategy of "putting pressure on Ukraine's position" at the negotiations. The Ukrainian military said on Tuesday that Russia had fired 162 drones and one ballistic missile overnight. Russia and Ukraine have held several rounds of failed talks during almost five years of war and hopes for peace are low. "We don't have any particular expectations," a senior Ukrainian official in Kyiv told AFP.

passages: ABU DHABI: US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Washington calling for a “new” security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent’s future.

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators sat facing each other, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff at the head of the table, in the first such talks since February in Geneva. Kushner said the US hoped to “create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding” that would secure “decades, if not centuries, of peace”.

The head of Moscow’s delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, said he hoped Moscow’s “bigger and more professional” team would “enable us to move forwards on the path towards peace”. A source in the Russian team said the Ukraine settlement was “merely one item on the agenda”, with the main objective “the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent”. The delegation includes, for the first time, diplomat Sergei Ryabkov, who issued Moscow’s ultimatum to the West on European security before the 2022 invasion.

Ukraine’s top negotiator Rustem Umerov said Kyiv’s priority remained securing a ceasefire and discussing security guarantees. “Our people are waiting to end this war,” he said. Before the talks, Ukraine’s delegation met the US envoys and European and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) officials, including NATO’s top commander in Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, who is also taking part. In a joint statement, they reaffirmed their “shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture”.

Europe has been alarmed by Trump’s plans, and the European Union (EU) said on the eve of the talks that “meaningful” security discussions could only take place after a ceasefire. Putin has refused broader ceasefires and face-to-face talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump hinted ahead of the talks that Ukraine might have to give up land, saying: “They’re going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine.” Russia occupies large parts of Ukraine but has not seized the whole of the Donetsk region, and demands that Kyiv surrender the areas it still holds there.

Russia pounded Ukraine in the run-up to the talks, with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid. The Ukrainian military said Russia fired 162 drones and one ballistic missile overnight into Tuesday. “We don’t have any particular expectations,” a senior Ukrainian official told AFP. — AFP

sources.title: Apple tells its Support Community to STFU - The Register
passages: Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026.
Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5.
Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular.
The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination.
"We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products."
Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device?
Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions.
Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure.

extraction.body: The broader crypto market crash is putting $XRP ’s recovery prospects at risk, with the token struggling to hold above the crucial $1.10 support level. Selling pressure is intensifying as Binance trading data shows a deeply negative Cumulative Volume Delta (CVD), indicating that market sell orders are outweighing buy orders. As bearish pressure spreads across the crypto market, can $XRP price hold $1.10, or is another decline approaching? On-chain trading activity shows concern for $XRP bulls. The latest Binance Cumulative Volume Delta (CVD) reading stands at approximately -4.33 million $XRP , indicating that market sell orders are currently exceeding market buy orders. CVD tracks the difference between aggressive buying and selling activity. A negative reading suggests that sellers are executing more market orders than buyers, reflecting stronger immediate selling pressure. The 30-day average CVD stands near 0.70 million, highlighting a notable shift in trading activity compared with the recent average. This suggests that aggressive selling has become more pronounced on Binance. $XRP ’s latest price action shows a weakening short-term structure. After trading around the $1.10–$1.20 region, the token faced renewed selling pressure and moved toward the $1.10 support area. The latest decline also pushed the price below nearby support levels, suggesting buyers have struggled to maintain control. The $1.10 region is now a critical area to watch. A sustained hold above this level could help $XRP stabilize and attempt a recovery toward its previous trading range. However, a decisive breakdown could weaken the price structure further and expose the next major support near $0.99. $XRP ’s near-term outlook remains cautious as weakening price action coincides with negative CVD readings. The combination suggests sellers currently have the upper hand, while buying demand has yet to show enough strength to reverse the trend. A sustained defense of $1.10 could help $XRP establish a base and encourage a recovery attempt. However, continued selling pressure and a failure to attract fresh buying interest could expose the $0.99 region. A bullish shift would require more than a temporary price bounce. $XRP needs to regain its lost trading range and show a meaningful improvement in buying activity to indicate that market control is moving back toward buyers.

extraction.body: Residents from across Cambridge gathered Saturday morning to help shape the city’s approach to public safety in the first-ever civic assembly held in Massachusetts. Among the group was a woman approaching her 80th birthday who has lived in the same building in The Port for half a century, three Cambridge Rindge and Latin School students, a mental health clinician who moved from Chicago nearly two decades ago, a third-generation Cantabrigian living in West Cambridge a woman who values Cambridge’s walkability but feels unsafe when walking home late at night and a lifelong North Cambridge resident concerned about recent shootings in her neighborhood. All are among the 40 residents selected by lottery to reflect Cambridge’s demographics, and had volunteered to participate (each will receive a $1,000 stipend for completing the four sessions). They will weigh the future of the city’s ShotSpotter gunshot detection system and surveillance cameras in public parks. And they may help heal a city riven by a death some think might have been prevented had the sound detection system not been deactivated by Cambridge’s City Council May 18. “When this process is finished, I hope you have done more than just make recommendations about technology,” said the Rev. Dr. Jeremy Battle, senior pastor of The Avenue Fellowship and a member of the assembly’s advisory committee, which helps guide the process, review educational materials and ensure participants hear balanced perspectives. “I hope you will have strengthened the way the city of Cambridge listens to itself from this inaugural moment.” The civic assembly was set in motion Aug. 3, when the council voted 6-3 to temporarily restore ShotSpotter and gather citizens to help determine its future. The assembly will meet for seven hours a session over four Saturdays through Dec. 5, then present recommendations to the City Council. The council is not obligated to adopt them. The first session can be viewed here . They started with data. Cambridge Police Department crime analysts Meghan LaMonica and Rebecca Leonard reviewed local crime trends showing the city recorded 475 violent crimes in 2025, less than half its 1990 peak of 1,077, although serious crime has risen since reaching a 55-year low in 2019. Gun violence remains concentrated in a handful of neighborhoods. Of 134 confirmed gunfire incidents citywide between January 2014 and Oct. 15, 2026, 68 occurred in The Port, and that neighborhood together with Cambridgeport and Wellington-Harrington, accounted for roughly 70% of incidents. ShotSpotter covers approximately 1.25 square miles, or 18%, of Cambridge’s land area, encompassing much of those neighborhoods. Although that area accounted for 74% of confirmed shootings between July 2014 and May 2026, ShotSpotter detected only 58 of the 96 confirmed shootings within its coverage area, a rate of 60%. Between 2015 and 2025, 35% of ShotSpotter alerts corresponded to confirmed shootings, compared with 18% of gunfire-related 911 calls. Following upgrades in 2021, ShotSpotter’s confirmation rate rose to 53% between 2022 and 2025. “Just because an alert is unfounded, it does not definitively mean that a shooting did not occur,” Leonard said. “It just means there was no evidence located that there had been a shooting.” Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them. In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes. A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024. Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared. “These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.” Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties. Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence. He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use. Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier. “My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.” Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system. Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge. She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest. “ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.” Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations. Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit. Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence. In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement. “I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.” As a nonprofit, community-based independent publication, we rely on contributions from readers like you to fund our journalism. Though this may seem like a large increase, the true price was never really $25. Rather, neighbors without cars were paying part of the difference. Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them.

In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes.

A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024.

Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared.
“These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.”

Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties.

Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence.

He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use.
Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier.

“My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.”

Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system.

Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge.

She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest.

“ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.”

Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations.
Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit.

Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence.
In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement.

“I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.”

passages: Cambridge’s 40-person resident assembly on surveillance technology held its second meeting on Saturday — marking the halfway point before the body is set to deliver recommendations on surveillance and violence prevention efforts to the City Council.
But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department.
Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night.
The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence.
CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday.
But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents.
DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures.

The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly.
The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415.

Saturday’s meeting centered on outlining issues with existing surveillance technology — and the city’s broader response to residents’ concerns. The assembly was created as a response to concerns that the City Council had failed to listen to residents as it wavered over the future of ShotSpotter, the automatic gunshot detection system. The City Council voted to remove the technology in May, citing privacy concerns, and reversed the decision in August after the fatal shooting of 32-year-old Xavier Bautista, a Public Works Department employee. The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly. The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence. The Black Response, an activist group that has spent years pushing the city to end its use of ShotSpotter presented at Saturday’s meeting. “What kind of city do we want to live in?” Virginia Cuello, a member of The Black Response asked “One that pays for microphones and sends multiple officers to a loud noise, or one that invests in the people and services that keep us safe?” But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department. CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday. All three options included scaling the number of cameras based on the number of calls CPD has received at each location over the last two years. Pigeon Park received the most calls for service during the period, 370, followed by Danehy Park with 171. Russell Field saw 148, and Cambridge Common saw 139. The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415. The final proposal came at the highest price tag, suggesting an additional twenty-five cameras would cost more than $295,692. Under each proposal, the funding would come partially from a Department of Homeland Security Urban Area Security Initiative grant. Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night. “I like to walk sometimes at night, so when I go to the Charles River, they have a camera there, and I feel safe because I know there’s a camera,” Hussein said. But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents. Troy A. DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures. “How are we going to implement these properly? Whether it’s like having better surveillance with people, like monitoring the parks, as in like visiting the parks, better lighting, or better community engagement,” DaCosta said. The assembly is slated to convene two more times over the next month, to outline its priorities and draft recommendations to the City Council in early December. —Staff writer Shawn A. Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night.
The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence.
CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday.

extraction.body: Residents from across Cambridge gathered Saturday morning to help shape the city’s approach to public safety in the first-ever civic assembly held in Massachusetts. Among the group was a woman approaching her 80th birthday who has lived in the same building in The Port for half a century, three Cambridge Rindge and Latin School students, a mental health clinician who moved from Chicago nearly two decades ago, a third-generation Cantabrigian living in West Cambridge a woman who values Cambridge’s walkability but feels unsafe when walking home late at night and a lifelong North Cambridge resident concerned about recent shootings in her neighborhood. All are among the 40 residents selected by lottery to reflect Cambridge’s demographics, and had volunteered to participate (each will receive a $1,000 stipend for completing the four sessions). They will weigh the future of the city’s ShotSpotter gunshot detection system and surveillance cameras in public parks. And they may help heal a city riven by a death some think might have been prevented had the sound detection system not been deactivated by Cambridge’s City Council May 18. “When this process is finished, I hope you have done more than just make recommendations about technology,” said the Rev. Dr. Jeremy Battle, senior pastor of The Avenue Fellowship and a member of the assembly’s advisory committee, which helps guide the process, review educational materials and ensure participants hear balanced perspectives. “I hope you will have strengthened the way the city of Cambridge listens to itself from this inaugural moment.” The civic assembly was set in motion Aug. 3, when the council voted 6-3 to temporarily restore ShotSpotter and gather citizens to help determine its future. The assembly will meet for seven hours a session over four Saturdays through Dec. 5, then present recommendations to the City Council. The council is not obligated to adopt them. The first session can be viewed here . They started with data. Cambridge Police Department crime analysts Meghan LaMonica and Rebecca Leonard reviewed local crime trends showing the city recorded 475 violent crimes in 2025, less than half its 1990 peak of 1,077, although serious crime has risen since reaching a 55-year low in 2019. Gun violence remains concentrated in a handful of neighborhoods. Of 134 confirmed gunfire incidents citywide between January 2014 and Oct. 15, 2026, 68 occurred in The Port, and that neighborhood together with Cambridgeport and Wellington-Harrington, accounted for roughly 70% of incidents. ShotSpotter covers approximately 1.25 square miles, or 18%, of Cambridge’s land area, encompassing much of those neighborhoods. Although that area accounted for 74% of confirmed shootings between July 2014 and May 2026, ShotSpotter detected only 58 of the 96 confirmed shootings within its coverage area, a rate of 60%. Between 2015 and 2025, 35% of ShotSpotter alerts corresponded to confirmed shootings, compared with 18% of gunfire-related 911 calls. Following upgrades in 2021, ShotSpotter’s confirmation rate rose to 53% between 2022 and 2025. “Just because an alert is unfounded, it does not definitively mean that a shooting did not occur,” Leonard said. “It just means there was no evidence located that there had been a shooting.” Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them. In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes. A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024. Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared. “These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.” Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties. Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence. He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use. Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier. “My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.” Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system. Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge. She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest. “ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.” Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations. Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit. Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence. In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement. “I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.” As a nonprofit, community-based independent publication, we rely on contributions from readers like you to fund our journalism. Though this may seem like a large increase, the true price was never really $25. Rather, neighbors without cars were paying part of the difference. extraction.body: Cambridge’s 40-person resident assembly on surveillance technology held its second meeting on Saturday — marking the halfway point before the body is set to deliver recommendations on surveillance and violence prevention efforts to the City Council. Saturday’s meeting centered on outlining issues with existing surveillance technology — and the city’s broader response to residents’ concerns. The assembly was created as a response to concerns that the City Council had failed to listen to residents as it wavered over the future of ShotSpotter, the automatic gunshot detection system. The City Council voted to remove the technology in May, citing privacy concerns, and reversed the decision in August after the fatal shooting of 32-year-old Xavier Bautista, a Public Works Department employee. The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly. The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence. The Black Response, an activist group that has spent years pushing the city to end its use of ShotSpotter presented at Saturday’s meeting. “What kind of city do we want to live in?” Virginia Cuello, a member of The Black Response asked “One that pays for microphones and sends multiple officers to a loud noise, or one that invests in the people and services that keep us safe?” But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department. CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday. All three options included scaling the number of cameras based on the number of calls CPD has received at each location over the last two years. Pigeon Park received the most calls for service during the period, 370, followed by Danehy Park with 171. Russell Field saw 148, and Cambridge Common saw 139. The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415. The final proposal came at the highest price tag, suggesting an additional twenty-five cameras would cost more than $295,692. Under each proposal, the funding would come partially from a Department of Homeland Security Urban Area Security Initiative grant. Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night. “I like to walk sometimes at night, so when I go to the Charles River, they have a camera there, and I feel safe because I know there’s a camera,” Hussein said. But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents. Troy A. DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures. “How are we going to implement these properly? Whether it’s like having better surveillance with people, like monitoring the parks, as in like visiting the parks, better lighting, or better community engagement,” DaCosta said. The assembly is slated to convene two more times over the next month, to outline its priorities and draft recommendations to the City Council in early December. —Staff writer Shawn A. extraction.body: Procurement records reviewed by Reuters show a blacklisted Chinese university bought two Nvidia H200 chips and rented more, exposing gaps in export controls. A Chinese university on a United States export blacklist bought two of Nvidia's H200 artificial intelligence chips in October for 874,700 yuan, about $123,000, according to procurement records reviewed by Reuters. Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an, one of China's "Seven Sons of National Defence" institutions, bought the chips for its management school from a domestic supplier, Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, rather than from Nvidia. Reuters reported that the university also bought access to H200 and other restricted Nvidia processors this year through five contracts for rented computing capacity. Its cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, for servers containing eight H200 chips each. Other records show rented servers with eight A100 and eight A800 chips, and an April contract worth 375,000 yuan requiring at least 24 A100 chips for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. Reuters reviewed 26 procurement and corporate records from this year. The pattern reaches beyond one campus. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors for 769,800 yuan in September, and Beihang University, another defence-linked institution, bought four A800 chips for 489,000 yuan in April. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips separately for 344,000 yuan. Two government notices for the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences named suppliers of H800 and A800 computing services, one listing H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. The prices allow a direct comparison. Dividing the purchase price by two gives 437,350 yuan for a single H200, about $61,500 at the exchange rate implied by Reuters' own conversion. The seven-month rental of eight H200 chips cost 441,700 yuan, roughly the price of buying one chip outright, or about 7,900 yuan per chip per month. That comparison is calculated from the recorded prices and excludes hosting, power and support costs, which the records do not disclose. For a laboratory that needs computing power for a defined project, renting is the cheaper route, and it leaves no imported hardware for inspectors to trace. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced on 13 January that it would review licence applications for the Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X and similar chips case by case, provided security conditions were met. Applicants must show exports will not reduce global production capacity available to US customers, that the Chinese buyer has export-compliance procedures including customer screening, and that the product has passed independent third-party testing in the United States. The rule followed President Donald Trump's announcement of 8 December 2025. Under Secretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler said permitting H200 sales "under controlled conditions will strengthen the American technology ecosystem". That change did not lift the separate Entity List restrictions on Northwestern Polytechnical, which Reuters reports was listed in 2001 over alleged missile-proliferation activity and military research, with a policy of denial applied from 2019. Analysis published on 16 January by the AI policy research group IAPS argued the certifications are hard to verify and the security plans unenforceable once chips leave the United States. It estimated the volume rule could initially allow about 900,000 H200-equivalent chips. The policy caps exports of a chip model to China at under half of cumulative sales of that model for end use in the United States, and requires lists of proposed remote-access customers. IAPS said there is no kill switch on an H200 and little leverage once the hardware is in China. Domestic resale and rental sit beyond that reach. The records Reuters reviewed offered little information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operate. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment, and the universities named did not respond. No finding of an illegal export by Nvidia has been published, and the records do not establish one. Reuters reported that Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged chip-tracking requirements and greater oversight of exports. Until then, procurement notices remain the clearest public evidence of what reaches blacklisted buyers.

A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist. Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports. The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed. The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser ⁠⁠restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 ‌‌chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology. However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ⁠⁠that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research. US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI ⁠⁠chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports. This comes at a time of increased pressure on Nvidia’s Huang. Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO after his intimate relationship with Alice Huang, accused of working for Chinese intelligence, plunged the company into crisis. “The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I ⁠⁠just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico late on Tuesday. A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist. Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports. The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed. The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser ⁠⁠restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 ‌‌chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology. However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ⁠⁠that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research. US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI ⁠⁠chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports. This comes at a time of increased pressure on Nvidia’s Huang. Jensen Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe US national security or confidential information has been compromised. Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on Sunday into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.

extraction.body: Residents from across Cambridge gathered Saturday morning to help shape the city’s approach to public safety in the first-ever civic assembly held in Massachusetts. Among the group was a woman approaching her 80th birthday who has lived in the same building in The Port for half a century, three Cambridge Rindge and Latin School students, a mental health clinician who moved from Chicago nearly two decades ago, a third-generation Cantabrigian living in West Cambridge a woman who values Cambridge’s walkability but feels unsafe when walking home late at night and a lifelong North Cambridge resident concerned about recent shootings in her neighborhood. All are among the 40 residents selected by lottery to reflect Cambridge’s demographics, and had volunteered to participate (each will receive a $1,000 stipend for completing the four sessions). They will weigh the future of the city’s ShotSpotter gunshot detection system and surveillance cameras in public parks. And they may help heal a city riven by a death some think might have been prevented had the sound detection system not been deactivated by Cambridge’s City Council May 18. “When this process is finished, I hope you have done more than just make recommendations about technology,” said the Rev. Dr. Jeremy Battle, senior pastor of The Avenue Fellowship and a member of the assembly’s advisory committee, which helps guide the process, review educational materials and ensure participants hear balanced perspectives. “I hope you will have strengthened the way the city of Cambridge listens to itself from this inaugural moment.” The civic assembly was set in motion Aug. 3, when the council voted 6-3 to temporarily restore ShotSpotter and gather citizens to help determine its future. The assembly will meet for seven hours a session over four Saturdays through Dec. 5, then present recommendations to the City Council. The council is not obligated to adopt them. The first session can be viewed here . They started with data. Cambridge Police Department crime analysts Meghan LaMonica and Rebecca Leonard reviewed local crime trends showing the city recorded 475 violent crimes in 2025, less than half its 1990 peak of 1,077, although serious crime has risen since reaching a 55-year low in 2019. Gun violence remains concentrated in a handful of neighborhoods. Of 134 confirmed gunfire incidents citywide between January 2014 and Oct. 15, 2026, 68 occurred in The Port, and that neighborhood together with Cambridgeport and Wellington-Harrington, accounted for roughly 70% of incidents. ShotSpotter covers approximately 1.25 square miles, or 18%, of Cambridge’s land area, encompassing much of those neighborhoods. Although that area accounted for 74% of confirmed shootings between July 2014 and May 2026, ShotSpotter detected only 58 of the 96 confirmed shootings within its coverage area, a rate of 60%. Between 2015 and 2025, 35% of ShotSpotter alerts corresponded to confirmed shootings, compared with 18% of gunfire-related 911 calls. Following upgrades in 2021, ShotSpotter’s confirmation rate rose to 53% between 2022 and 2025. “Just because an alert is unfounded, it does not definitively mean that a shooting did not occur,” Leonard said. “It just means there was no evidence located that there had been a shooting.” Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them. In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes. A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024. Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared. “These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.” Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties. Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence. He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use. Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier. “My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.” Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system. Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge. She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest. “ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.” Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations. Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit. Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence. In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement. “I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.” As a nonprofit, community-based independent publication, we rely on contributions from readers like you to fund our journalism. On December 1, Cambridge residents can start renewing their resident parking permits, and for the first time since 2013, the price is going up, from $25 to $75. Though this may seem like a large increase, the true price was never really $25. Rather, neighbors without cars were paying part of the difference. But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department.
Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night.

CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday.
But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents.
DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures.

Saturday’s meeting centered on outlining issues with existing surveillance technology — and the city’s broader response to residents’ concerns. The City Council voted to remove the technology in May, citing privacy concerns, and reversed the decision in August after the fatal shooting of 32-year-old Xavier Bautista, a Public Works Department employee. The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly. The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence. The Black Response, an activist group that has spent years pushing the city to end its use of ShotSpotter presented at Saturday’s meeting. “What kind of city do we want to live in?” Virginia Cuello, a member of The Black Response asked “One that pays for microphones and sends multiple officers to a loud noise, or one that invests in the people and services that keep us safe?” But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department. All three options included scaling the number of cameras based on the number of calls CPD has received at each location over the last two years. Pigeon Park received the most calls for service during the period, 370, followed by Danehy Park with 171. Russell Field saw 148, and Cambridge Common saw 139. The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415. The final proposal came at the highest price tag, suggesting an additional twenty-five cameras would cost more than $295,692. Under each proposal, the funding would come partially from a Department of Homeland Security Urban Area Security Initiative grant. Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night. “I like to walk sometimes at night, so when I go to the Charles River, they have a camera there, and I feel safe because I know there’s a camera,” Hussein said. But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents. Troy A. DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures. “How are we going to implement these properly? Whether it’s like having better surveillance with people, like monitoring the parks, as in like visiting the parks, better lighting, or better community engagement,” DaCosta said.
