extraction.body: Huang faces a board probe as investors fret over Nvidia’s lack of a clear successor. The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company. Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy. The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 percent by midday trading on Monday. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post. Nvidia’s chips were instrumental in the creation of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and now sit at the center of Big Tech’s $1 trillion AI infrastructure frenzy. Huang has personally stood behind investments and guarantees running into hundreds of billions of dollars for dozens of AI start-ups and data center providers, as well as lobbying US President Donald Trump for looser AI regulation. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” analysts at Bernstein said in a note to clients. With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend. The investigation will probably be led by board member and former Cooley chief executive Stephen C. Neal, according to people familiar with the probe. “If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position. “Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.” In contrast to other leading Big Tech companies, Nvidia’s annual reports and corporate governance paperwork make no specific reference to “succession planning” and set out no details for how it would replace its CEO, even in an emergency, beyond noting that the company “believe[s] in extensive leadership development.” Huang’s unusually large number of direct reports, numbered at more than 60 according to a 2024 disclosure, present Nvidia’s board with a “pool of excellent candidates for future promotion,” recent filings say. Huang leads a small core executive team at Nvidia, including Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, Operations Chief Debora Shoquist and general counsel Tim Teter. He has become one of Huang’s closest lieutenants since joining in 2017 and has lobbied Washington on export controls. Jay Puri, a close lieutenant who led Nvidia’s sales operations and deputized for Huang on international visits, stepped down in August and was replaced on the executive team by Microsoft veteran Nick Parker. Huang, who has cultivated an air of infallibility inside Nvidia, has given no indication he will step down from the role of CEO. Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine , portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership. He is known to be able to inspire extraordinary productivity inside a company whose 42,000 employees each generated an average of more than $7 million in annual revenue over the past 12 months, far more than any other Big Tech group. But Kim also notes that Huang represents the company’s “single point of failure,” functioning as its head of marketing, sales, and product development. His influence in the wider tech industry is also unique. Endorsements by Huang of companies in the AI semiconductor supply chain can supercharge their share prices, while his offhand dismissal early last year of the near-term commercial prospects for quantum computing sent stocks in the sector spiraling. Despite his imperial stature, Huang owns just 3.6 percent of Nvidia. That stake makes him Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder and is worth more than $150 billion. However, Huang lacks the special voting rights held by many Silicon Valley founders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, that would allow him to control the board or face down outside investors who might attempt to oust him. Huang’s total compensation last year of $36.3 million, of which the vast majority came in the form of stock awards, included some $4 million for security paid for by Nvidia, which filings say is “due to the exceptionally high public profile and prominence of our CEO.” These costs included protection at home and during “personal travel,” as well as using private aircraft for all business trips, according to filings. Huang reimburses Nvidia for personal air travel on private aircraft arranged by the company, according to filings. Nvidia’s board, whose individual members have until now kept a low profile, confirmed they would appoint a special committee composed of sitting board members assisted by outside counsel to examine the allegations surrounding its CEO. Neal joined Nvidia’s board in 2019 and is chair emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, after serving as the law firm’s CEO from 2001 to 2008. Nvidia’s board is unusual among the largest US companies in having no designated chair. A 2025 report by law firm Fenwick found that only one company in S&P 100—which would be Nvidia, according to its own filings—had no chair. In its proxy filings, Nvidia states that this set-up “ensures that each member has an equal voice in the affairs and management of Nvidia.” The other nine members of Nvidia’s board—excluding Huang, who is himself a director—include four men who have been with the company since the 1990s, a former Taco Bell executive, a professor of aeronautics, and a former Goldman Sachs executive who joined only this year. The board’s public statement on Sunday said it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team” and that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Nonetheless, his admission of an affair on Sunday shocked employees and former colleagues who spoke to the FT. Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter who serves as a senior director in Nvidia’s product marketing team and has become an increasingly visible presence at the company’s conferences, canceled a planned appearance at a company event in South Korea on Monday. The law in Delaware, where Nvidia is incorporated, says executives have certain fiduciary duties including a duty of care and loyalty to their company. Nvidia’s code of conduct requires executives to “conduct themselves with the highest degree of integrity, ethics and honesty. Our credibility and reputation depend upon their good judgment, ethical standards and personal integrity.” Even if Huang is found to have breached those guidelines, his defenders in Silicon Valley argue that he is too big to fire. “Yes he should have known better,” Sequoia’s Maguire said. “But let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op.”

sources.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
passages: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws.
The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027.

It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports.
On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University.
The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks.
Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital.
The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed.

Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm.
Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits.

The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027. The RAISE Act , New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports. The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics. “Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.” On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. extraction.body: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws. The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027. The RAISE Act , New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports. The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics. “Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.” On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits. extraction.body: David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI) , used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing. “I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?” The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution. The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said. More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving. “A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?” That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding. “An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.” For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies. “Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.” Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation. “At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible. “If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.” As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it. “As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.” “We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

extraction.body: David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI) , used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing. “I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?” The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution. The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said. More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving. “A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?” That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding. “An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.” For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies. “Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.” Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation. “At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible. “If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.” As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it. “As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.” “We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

passages: LONDON, October 05, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--New research from FICO (NYSE: FICO), a leading global analytics software firm, shows that fraud leaders across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) are grappling with rising fraud complexity and AI-enabled threats, even as they accelerate investment in AI-driven detection and enterprise-wide fraud strategy.

The findings, drawn from FICO's global survey of 202 senior fraud, risk and technology professionals at retail banks, neobanks and fintechs, show that 52% of EMEA institutions now cite increasing fraud complexity as their leading fraud prevention challenge, compared with just 40% of global firms.
And nearly half ranked effective AI integration as a top challenge, underscoring that embedding AI into existing fraud controls remains as much an operational hurdle as a technological one.
"Fraud in EMEA is not accelerating out of control, but it is becoming far more sophisticated, and that shift matters just as much," said Adam Davies, vice president, Product Management at FICO .

The findings, drawn from FICO's global survey of 202 senior fraud, risk and technology professionals at retail banks, neobanks and fintechs, show that 52% of EMEA institutions now cite increasing fraud complexity as their leading fraud prevention challenge, compared with just 40% of global firms. And nearly half ranked effective AI integration as a top challenge, underscoring that embedding AI into existing fraud controls remains as much an operational hurdle as a technological one.
More than one-third (36%) of EMEA institutions report fraud attempts rising by more than 25% over the past 24 months
28% reported that financial losses from fraud grew more than 25% over the past 2 years
Effective AI integration ranks as a top challenge for 48% of EMEA respondents, closely mirroring the global response

"Fraud in EMEA is not accelerating out of control, but it is becoming far more sophisticated, and that shift matters just as much," said Adam Davies, vice president, Product Management at FICO . "Fraudsters now have access to the same generative and agentic AI tools that banks are deploying to stop them, and they are using them to scale social engineering, synthetic identities and deepfake-enabled attacks. The institutions pulling ahead are the ones connecting their fraud functions across the enterprise and orchestrating every intelligence source they have, rather than adding point solutions one at a time."
Other highlights from the FICO research for EMEA:

EMEA respondents rate AI-enhanced fraud (4.42 out of 5) and social engineering scams (4.36) as more significant threats than the global average (3.86 and 3.90 respectively), with synthetic identities (4.02) and deepfake fraud (3.96) also outpacing global concern levels
86% of EMEA institutions see a unified, enterprise-wide fraud strategy as essential, with 38% already treating it as a critical priority and 48% pursuing it as a longer-term focus
Half (51%) of EMEA institutions report false positive rates above 15%, creating friction for legitimate customers even as fraud controls tighten

Third-party vendor models now carry the greatest influence over EMEA fraud decisions (46%), far more than in-house models (24%), reflecting growing reliance on external expertise to keep pace with evolving threats

"The next 24 months will be defined by orchestration, not by any single piece of technology," Davies added. "EMEA institutions have already built strong foundations in AI-driven detection, and confidence in agentic AI is particularly high in the region. What's needed now is the connective tissue: bringing in-house models, vendor intelligence and consortium data together so fraud teams can act on a complete picture in real time, without pushing more friction onto legitimate customers."
Davies points out four priorities for financial institutions in their fight against fraud:

Close the deployment gap by moving AI from pilot to production at enterprise scale. "You should prioritize what works within disciplined fraud control frameworks rather than launching yet more pilots," he noted.
Invest in active orchestration across models, channels, products, and portfolios so that shared signals shape fraud management decisions in real time.
Apply risk-based, outcome-driven prioritization to balance competing investment demands, led by financial impact and regulatory exposure.
Treat fraud prevention and customer experience as a single, connected challenge. "The organizations that can do both will be the ones that define competitive advantage in this era," Davies said.

FICO® Enterprise Fraud Solution, powered by FICO® Platform , addresses the full spectrum of fraud, from synthetic identity and application fraud to real-time payment scams and account takeover. passages: Shane Riedman (pictured), president of anti-fraud analytics at the data analytics firm, told Insurance Business the convergence of widespread AI tools and shifting consumer attitudes, especially among the younger generations, has created a “perfect storm” for insurers.

It’s the combination of those two things – the willingness and the availability of the tools – that is creating a lot of fear and anxiety in the insurance market today.” The research highlights what Riedman describes as an “ethics gap,” where everyday use of AI editing tools (like adjusting lighting or removing elements from images) has blurred the line between acceptable behavior and fraud. Nearly half of consumers who have used AI editing tools said their results looked “very realistic,” while 62% believe AI is already frequently used to manipulate insurance claims . The impact is tangible for insurers. Early deepfake detection systems have achieved near-perfect accuracy, according to Riedman, only to be quickly surpassed by evolving fraud techniques. The challenge is compounded by the broader technology landscape. Consumer-facing AI tools developed by companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Meta are widely accessible and increasingly sophisticated, lowering the barrier to entry for would-be fraudsters. Even collaborative efforts, such as embedding watermarks in AI-generated images, have proven difficult to enforce, as bad actors find ways to bypass safeguards. “This isn’t just insurers versus individual fraudsters,” Riedman said. “We’re effectively up against an entire ecosystem of rapidly evolving technology.” The rise in AI-driven fraud is expected to have ripple effects across the insurance ecosystem, particularly for brokers and their clients. According to the study, 69% of consumers believe fraud will ultimately lead to higher premiums. Riedman agreed, noting that increased claims costs and fraud detection investments will inevitably be passed on. “Property and casualty insurers operate on very thin margins,” Riedman said. “When you increase costs on the claims side, that money has to come from somewhere… and it typically comes from premiums.” Beyond pricing, customer experience is also set to change. extraction.body: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed numerous sectors, including finance, medicine, education, and the automotive insurance industry, which is no exception. Yet, as with all transformative technologies, AI’s rapid adoption comes with both promise and peril. One of the most alarming developments we’re now confronting is the systemic exploitation of AI for fraudulent insurance claims within the automotive sector. It’s a problem that is escalating, difficult to detect, and, for now, largely unpunished. Example 1: The system has identified and linked the images in which the damage partially overlaps. On the corner of the bumper trim, there are characteristic cracks indicated by arrows. However, in the photo from the more recent damage, there is also a dent in the fender. Example 2: An artificial intelligence algorithm identified identical damage to the rear lamp occurring on two different vehicles. My team and I at ControlExpert have spent the last three years studying this phenomenon in the Polish market, and our findings are both fascinating and concerning. What began as a curiosity about why damaged car parts, such as headlights or bumpers, are sold in sets online quickly led us to uncover an ecosystem of professional fraud. These damaged parts, often beyond repair, serve a very specific purpose: they’re used to stage insurance claims with “evidence” of collisions that never happened. After the claim is approved and paid out, the original, undamaged parts are reinstalled. The result? A clean car, a closed claim, and a fraudulent payout. Example 3: Re-reported damage detected thanks to the FOTO system. Damage reported under third-party liability insurance more than 6 months apart. Example 4: Damage related by the PHOTO system, in which the damage to the trunk lid is identical. On the other hand, in the case of damage reported almost a year later (below), the damage in the bumper area is smaller than in the older damage (photo above). “The FOTO system was a unique project for us – both in terms of data volume and impact. We are proud to provide a scalable market-wide solution that specifically helps to prevent abuse,” says Grzegorz Czekiel, President of the Management Board of ControlExpert Polska. “The consolidated effort of almost the entire insurance market under the leadership of UFG is a huge step forward.” This isn’t theoretical. We discovered examples where body shops reused the same damage photos in dozens of claims. In one case, a photo of a damaged bumper was used in over 40 separate claims. We’ve even identified images of cracked windshields appearing in claims for vehicles of entirely different makes, ages, and specifications. And these aren’t isolated incidents. The frequency and scale suggest something more industrial than incidental: a fraud factory fueled by digital manipulation. What’s most troubling is that these acts are not committed by amateur fraudsters working in isolation. Instead, they are orchestrated by professional repair shops, entities we trust to fix our vehicles, who are now using AI tools to generate, alter, and replicate images as part of their revenue streams. For them, this is simply an extension of their business model. Repairing cars and gaming the system have become two sides of the same coin. As AI continues to democratise, so too does the capability to deceive. Modern generative tools can fabricate realistic damage with shocking ease. Tutorials are circulating on social media showing users how to edit images of their undamaged vehicles to simulate crashes, all under the pretence of harmless pranks, though the implications are far more serious. For less than the cost of a dinner out, one can purchase a suite of modified “accident” photos designed to trick insurers. Worse still, many of these low-level frauds go unpunished. If a fraudulent claim is rejected, there are no legal repercussions. This absence of accountability emboldens others. As the risk diminishes and the ease increases, more and more people, both individuals and businesses, are tempted to test the system. Even worse, insurance providers often remain silent, unwilling to reveal the scale of the issue due to reputational concerns. AI should have been the silver bullet for efficiency and objectivity in claims processing. Instead, it has created a new loophole, one that’s being exploited faster than we can seal it. That said, we are not without hope. Strategies are underway to mitigate this crisis. As a result of the initiative of the Polish Chamber of Insurers and the Polish Guarantee Fund, we’ve implemented a centralised database that collects millions of claim images. By leveraging AI to scan for patterns and similarities, we can identify suspicious images that have been reused or damaged elements occurring in other claims. We are also collaborating with the Polish Guarantee Fund to train detection models that distinguish between authentic and altered photos. These initiatives offer a glimmer of defence, but they’re only part of the solution. What we truly need is a united front: collaboration across borders, across companies, and across sectors. Insurance companies must be willing to share data, even sensitive data, to build more robust fraud detection frameworks. Governments must consider legal reforms that allow for stricter penalties on claim fraud, even on a small scale. And the tech industry must accelerate the development of tamper-evident image capture standards, such as digital signatures embedded in photos, that make forgery easier to detect. Until then, the AI fraud arms race will continue. For every advancement we make in detection, those seeking to exploit the system will move two steps ahead. But with vigilance, innovation, and cooperation, we can still close the gap. We owe it to the vast majority of honest claimants and to the financial sustainability of our insurance systems not to let technology’s promise become its downfall. Pablo Hernandez de Cos reiterated a warning delivered by his institution in June, observing that investors’ hopes pinned to the technology have driven “elevated” stock valuations based on “ambitious expectations.” “Should the returns to AI disappoint, a pullback in investment could turn today’s capital expenditure boom into a bust,” he told an event in Mumbai on Thursday. “The consequences of such a correction could be larger than in the past.” Several global policymakers have rung alarm bells on the matter this year. Among the most recent was Financial Stability Board Chair Andrew Bailey, who cited the danger of a “ disorderly correction that could spread across borders.” “A key feature of the AI market that raises the risk of such a bust is the investment arms race between AI firms,” de Cos said. “Driven by intense competition, these firms risk over-investing resources.” He listed the 1830s canal mania, Britain’s 1840s railway mania, the electrification boom of the 1920s and the dotcom bubble of the 1990s as relevant past examples. “In each of these cases, the eventual correction that followed had economy-wide implications,” he said. On the eve of his speech, Fitch Ratings published one possible such scenario, featuring a 35% drop in US stocks over a period of half a year. That would result in an American recession and “a very sharp slowdown” in global growth, economists Alex Muscatelli, Brian Coulton and Zazral Purewsuren wrote in a report. De Cos reckons this time could be different from prior crashes because of greater consumer investments in stocks that could then hurt spending, more of a global focus on US equities, and the possibility of domestic asset bubbles caused by local AI-related export booms. The dynamics of the current situation pose particular risks, he added, noting that AI investment is concentrating among only a few players, and capital spending outpaces cashflow at such companies, prompting them to rely on debt and private credit. Moreover, a lot of that activity is “opaque and interconnected.” “I do not say that this is where the AI boom must lead,” he said. “But the scale and speed of the current investment boom, and the weight of expected commercial returns, do warrant some caution.” De Cos also cited the separate stability risk to cyber security, noting prior research that suggests AI could “tilt the balance in favor of attackers.” A former Bank of Spain governor, de Cos is a possible successor to European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde. coreStoryFacts.text: LONDON, October 05, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--New research from FICO (NYSE: FICO), a leading global analytics software firm, shows that fraud leaders across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) are grappling with rising fraud complexity and AI-enabled threats, even as they accelerate investment in AI-driven detection and enterprise-wide fraud strategy.

The findings, drawn from FICO's global survey of 202 senior fraud, risk and technology professionals at retail banks, neobanks and fintechs, show that 52% of EMEA institutions now cite increasing fraud complexity as their leading fraud prevention challenge, compared with just 40% of global firms.
And nearly half ranked effective AI integration as a top challenge, underscoring that embedding AI into existing fraud controls remains as much an operational hurdle as a technological one.
"Fraud in EMEA is not accelerating out of control, but it is becoming far more sophisticated, and that shift matters just as much," said Adam Davies, vice president, Product Management at FICO .

"Fraudsters now have access to the same generative and agentic AI tools that banks are deploying to stop them, and they are using them to scale social engineering, synthetic identities and deepfake-enabled attacks.

The institutions pulling ahead are the ones connecting their fraud functions across the enterprise and orchestrating every intelligence source they have, rather than adding point solutions one at a time."
Other highlights from the FICO research for EMEA:

Third-party vendor models now carry the greatest influence over EMEA fraud decisions (46%), far more than in-house models (24%), reflecting growing reliance on external expertise to keep pace with evolving threats
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"The next 24 months will be defined by orchestration, not by any single piece of technology," Davies added.
FICO® Enterprise Fraud Solution, powered by FICO® Platform , addresses the full spectrum of fraud, from synthetic identity and application fraud to real-time payment scams and account takeover.

Shane Riedman (pictured), president of anti-fraud analytics at the data analytics firm, told Insurance Business the convergence of widespread AI tools and shifting consumer attitudes, especially among the younger generations, has created a “perfect storm” for insurers.
This dynamic, he said, is already driving operational changes and could significantly impact policyholders.
Verisk found nearly all carriers surveyed (98%) said AI-powered tools are fueling a rise in digital fraud, and 76% reported that manipulated claims have become more sophisticated in the past year.

Increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence (AI) tools are accelerating insurance fraud at a pace that is reshaping claims, trust, and pricing across the industry, according to new research and commentary from Verisk .
Verisk’s latest State of Insurance Fraud study found that 55% of Gen Z respondents would consider altering claim evidence, compared with just 12% of baby boomers.

Riedman warned that many consumers do not fully understand the broader consequences of these actions. “We’re doing a poor job as an industry educating people about the importance of insurance,” he said. “When someone inflates a claim or fabricates evidence, they’re not just affecting an insurer, they’re impacting their neighbors and the broader system.”
Despite heavy investment in AI-powered fraud detection, insurers are locked in a continuous battle with fraudsters.
The rise in AI-driven fraud is expected to have ripple effects across the insurance ecosystem, particularly for brokers and their clients.

Insurance companies must be willing to share data, even sensitive data, to build more robust fraud detection frameworks.

The findings, drawn from FICO's global survey of 202 senior fraud, risk and technology professionals at retail banks, neobanks and fintechs, show that 52% of EMEA institutions now cite increasing fraud complexity as their leading fraud prevention challenge, compared with just 40% of global firms.
And nearly half ranked effective AI integration as a top challenge, underscoring that embedding AI into existing fraud controls remains as much an operational hurdle as a technological one.
"Fraud in EMEA is not accelerating out of control, but it is becoming far more sophisticated, and that shift matters just as much," said Adam Davies, vice president, Product Management at FICO .

"Fraudsters now have access to the same generative and agentic AI tools that banks are deploying to stop them, and they are using them to scale social engineering, synthetic identities and deepfake-enabled attacks.

Shane Riedman (pictured), president of anti-fraud analytics at the data analytics firm, told Insurance Business the convergence of widespread AI tools and shifting consumer attitudes, especially among the younger generations, has created a “perfect storm” for insurers. This dynamic, he said, is already driving operational changes and could significantly impact policyholders. Verisk’s latest State of Insurance Fraud study found that 55% of Gen Z respondents would consider altering claim evidence, compared with just 12% of baby boomers. Across all age groups, more than one-third of consumers said they would consider digitally modifying claim materials. “What was really shocking was seeing that number at more than half of Generation Z,” Riedman said of the study. “We would have expected something closer to 10% or the teens. “What we’re seeing is that the wide proliferation of AI tools, and the ready availability of those tools, is arming the average Gen Zer to be able to very quickly and easily – and, in their minds, somewhat innocently – commit insurance fraud. It’s the combination of those two things – the willingness and the availability of the tools – that is creating a lot of fear and anxiety in the insurance market today.” The research highlights what Riedman describes as an “ethics gap,” where everyday use of AI editing tools (like adjusting lighting or removing elements from images) has blurred the line between acceptable behavior and fraud. Nearly half of consumers who have used AI editing tools said their results looked “very realistic,” while 62% believe AI is already frequently used to manipulate insurance claims . The impact is tangible for insurers. Verisk found nearly all carriers surveyed (98%) said AI-powered tools are fueling a rise in digital fraud, and 76% reported that manipulated claims have become more sophisticated in the past year. Riedman warned that many consumers do not fully understand the broader consequences of these actions. “We’re doing a poor job as an industry educating people about the importance of insurance,” he said. “When someone inflates a claim or fabricates evidence, they’re not just affecting an insurer, they’re impacting their neighbors and the broader system.” Despite heavy investment in AI-powered fraud detection, insurers are locked in a continuous battle with fraudsters. Early deepfake detection systems have achieved near-perfect accuracy, according to Riedman, only to be quickly surpassed by evolving fraud techniques. The challenge is compounded by the broader technology landscape. Consumer-facing AI tools developed by companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Meta are widely accessible and increasingly sophisticated, lowering the barrier to entry for would-be fraudsters. Even collaborative efforts, such as embedding watermarks in AI-generated images, have proven difficult to enforce, as bad actors find ways to bypass safeguards. “This isn’t just insurers versus individual fraudsters,” Riedman said. “We’re effectively up against an entire ecosystem of rapidly evolving technology.” The rise in AI-driven fraud is expected to have ripple effects across the insurance ecosystem, particularly for brokers and their clients. According to the study, 69% of consumers believe fraud will ultimately lead to higher premiums. Riedman agreed, noting that increased claims costs and fraud detection investments will inevitably be passed on. “Property and casualty insurers operate on very thin margins,” Riedman said. “When you increase costs on the claims side, that money has to come from somewhere… and it typically comes from premiums.” Beyond pricing, customer experience is also set to change. As trust in submitted evidence declines, insurers are introducing additional layers of scrutiny, which could slow claims processing and increase friction. Riedman said carriers are increasingly shifting toward structured, app-based claims workflows, where documents and images are submitted through controlled environments that enable real-time fraud checks. “There’s going to be more skepticism around every claim,” Riedman said. “Even legitimate claimants will feel that through longer processing times and more reviews.” With no single company able to solve the issue alone, insurers are increasingly calling for greater collaboration and data sharing. Riedman said carriers are recognizing the need to pool intelligence, including known fraudulent images and claims patterns, to stay ahead of organized schemes. “We believe strongly that technology on its own is not going to solve the problem. But when you bring them all together – multiple carriers, multiple technologies, and multiple vendors who are all aiming to defend the market – that’s where we find strength,” he said. “We also have to recognize that the bad actors are communicating with each other. There are open forums where they share technology and techniques for defrauding insurers.” There is also a growing role for brokers in combating fraud, particularly through client education and carrier selection. Brokers need to help customers understand the risks and the broader impact of fraud, said Riedman: “It should be part of the conversation, just like any other risk exposure.” Amidst this shift, brokers and agents can differentiate themselves by incorporating anti-fraud considerations into their advisory services and steering clients toward carriers with strong fraud detection capabilities. “I don’t think we consistently see that in the broker world. Traditionally, it has been risk assessment and delivering a solution,” Riedman said. “But I think going one step further with education, ensuring customers are fully aware of the risks and understand some of the defenses their carrier is putting into play, is crucial.” We'll keep you up-to-date with the latest breaking news, cutting edge opinion, and expert analysis affecting both your business and the industry as whole.

extraction.body: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed numerous sectors, including finance, medicine, education, and the automotive insurance industry, which is no exception. Yet, as with all transformative technologies, AI’s rapid adoption comes with both promise and peril. One of the most alarming developments we’re now confronting is the systemic exploitation of AI for fraudulent insurance claims within the automotive sector. It’s a problem that is escalating, difficult to detect, and, for now, largely unpunished. Example 1: The system has identified and linked the images in which the damage partially overlaps. On the corner of the bumper trim, there are characteristic cracks indicated by arrows. However, in the photo from the more recent damage, there is also a dent in the fender. Example 2: An artificial intelligence algorithm identified identical damage to the rear lamp occurring on two different vehicles. My team and I at ControlExpert have spent the last three years studying this phenomenon in the Polish market, and our findings are both fascinating and concerning. What began as a curiosity about why damaged car parts, such as headlights or bumpers, are sold in sets online quickly led us to uncover an ecosystem of professional fraud. These damaged parts, often beyond repair, serve a very specific purpose: they’re used to stage insurance claims with “evidence” of collisions that never happened. After the claim is approved and paid out, the original, undamaged parts are reinstalled. The result? A clean car, a closed claim, and a fraudulent payout. Example 3: Re-reported damage detected thanks to the FOTO system. Damage reported under third-party liability insurance more than 6 months apart. Example 4: Damage related by the PHOTO system, in which the damage to the trunk lid is identical. On the other hand, in the case of damage reported almost a year later (below), the damage in the bumper area is smaller than in the older damage (photo above). “The FOTO system was a unique project for us – both in terms of data volume and impact. We are proud to provide a scalable market-wide solution that specifically helps to prevent abuse,” says Grzegorz Czekiel, President of the Management Board of ControlExpert Polska. “The consolidated effort of almost the entire insurance market under the leadership of UFG is a huge step forward.” This isn’t theoretical. We discovered examples where body shops reused the same damage photos in dozens of claims. In one case, a photo of a damaged bumper was used in over 40 separate claims. We’ve even identified images of cracked windshields appearing in claims for vehicles of entirely different makes, ages, and specifications. And these aren’t isolated incidents. The frequency and scale suggest something more industrial than incidental: a fraud factory fueled by digital manipulation. What’s most troubling is that these acts are not committed by amateur fraudsters working in isolation. Instead, they are orchestrated by professional repair shops, entities we trust to fix our vehicles, who are now using AI tools to generate, alter, and replicate images as part of their revenue streams. For them, this is simply an extension of their business model. Repairing cars and gaming the system have become two sides of the same coin. As AI continues to democratise, so too does the capability to deceive. Modern generative tools can fabricate realistic damage with shocking ease. Tutorials are circulating on social media showing users how to edit images of their undamaged vehicles to simulate crashes, all under the pretence of harmless pranks, though the implications are far more serious. For less than the cost of a dinner out, one can purchase a suite of modified “accident” photos designed to trick insurers. Worse still, many of these low-level frauds go unpunished. If a fraudulent claim is rejected, there are no legal repercussions. This absence of accountability emboldens others. As the risk diminishes and the ease increases, more and more people, both individuals and businesses, are tempted to test the system. Even worse, insurance providers often remain silent, unwilling to reveal the scale of the issue due to reputational concerns. AI should have been the silver bullet for efficiency and objectivity in claims processing. Instead, it has created a new loophole, one that’s being exploited faster than we can seal it. That said, we are not without hope. Strategies are underway to mitigate this crisis. As a result of the initiative of the Polish Chamber of Insurers and the Polish Guarantee Fund, we’ve implemented a centralised database that collects millions of claim images. By leveraging AI to scan for patterns and similarities, we can identify suspicious images that have been reused or damaged elements occurring in other claims. We are also collaborating with the Polish Guarantee Fund to train detection models that distinguish between authentic and altered photos. These initiatives offer a glimmer of defence, but they’re only part of the solution. What we truly need is a united front: collaboration across borders, across companies, and across sectors. Insurance companies must be willing to share data, even sensitive data, to build more robust fraud detection frameworks. Governments must consider legal reforms that allow for stricter penalties on claim fraud, even on a small scale. And the tech industry must accelerate the development of tamper-evident image capture standards, such as digital signatures embedded in photos, that make forgery easier to detect. Until then, the AI fraud arms race will continue. For every advancement we make in detection, those seeking to exploit the system will move two steps ahead. But with vigilance, innovation, and cooperation, we can still close the gap. We owe it to the vast majority of honest claimants and to the financial sustainability of our insurance systems not to let technology’s promise become its downfall. extraction.body: The artificial intelligence boom remains a global financial stability danger that risks more damage than past crashes, the Bank for International Settlements chief said. Pablo Hernandez de Cos reiterated a warning delivered by his institution in June, observing that investors’ hopes pinned to the technology have driven “elevated” stock valuations based on “ambitious expectations.” “Should the returns to AI disappoint, a pullback in investment could turn today’s capital expenditure boom into a bust,” he told an event in Mumbai on Thursday. “The consequences of such a correction could be larger than in the past.” Several global policymakers have rung alarm bells on the matter this year. Among the most recent was Financial Stability Board Chair Andrew Bailey, who cited the danger of a “ disorderly correction that could spread across borders.” “A key feature of the AI market that raises the risk of such a bust is the investment arms race between AI firms,” de Cos said. “Driven by intense competition, these firms risk over-investing resources.” He listed the 1830s canal mania, Britain’s 1840s railway mania, the electrification boom of the 1920s and the dotcom bubble of the 1990s as relevant past examples. “In each of these cases, the eventual correction that followed had economy-wide implications,” he said. On the eve of his speech, Fitch Ratings published one possible such scenario, featuring a 35% drop in US stocks over a period of half a year. That would result in an American recession and “a very sharp slowdown” in global growth, economists Alex Muscatelli, Brian Coulton and Zazral Purewsuren wrote in a report. De Cos reckons this time could be different from prior crashes because of greater consumer investments in stocks that could then hurt spending, more of a global focus on US equities, and the possibility of domestic asset bubbles caused by local AI-related export booms. The dynamics of the current situation pose particular risks, he added, noting that AI investment is concentrating among only a few players, and capital spending outpaces cashflow at such companies, prompting them to rely on debt and private credit. Moreover, a lot of that activity is “opaque and interconnected.” “I do not say that this is where the AI boom must lead,” he said. “But the scale and speed of the current investment boom, and the weight of expected commercial returns, do warrant some caution.” De Cos also cited the separate stability risk to cyber security, noting prior research that suggests AI could “tilt the balance in favor of attackers.” A former Bank of Spain governor, de Cos is a possible successor to European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde. passages: The artificial intelligence boom remains a global financial stability danger that risks more damage than past crashes, the Bank for International Settlements chief said.

Pablo Hernandez de Cos reiterated a warning delivered by his institution in June, observing that investors’ hopes pinned to the technology have driven “elevated” stock valuations based on “ambitious expectations.”

“Should the returns to AI disappoint, a pullback in investment could turn today’s capital expenditure boom into a bust,” he told an event in Mumbai on Thursday. “The consequences of such a correction could be larger than in the past.”

Several global policymakers have rung alarm bells on the matter this year. Among the most recent was Financial Stability Board Chair Andrew Bailey, who cited the danger of a “ disorderly correction that could spread across borders.”

“A key feature of the AI market that raises the risk of such a bust is the investment arms race between AI firms,” de Cos said. “Driven by intense competition, these firms risk over-investing resources.”
He listed the 1830s canal mania, Britain’s 1840s railway mania, the electrification boom of the 1920s and the dotcom bubble of the 1990s as relevant past examples.
“In each of these cases, the eventual correction that followed had economy-wide implications,” he said.
On the eve of his speech, Fitch Ratings published one possible such scenario, featuring a 35% drop in US stocks over a period of half a year.
That would result in an American recession and “a very sharp slowdown” in global growth, economists Alex Muscatelli, Brian Coulton and Zazral Purewsuren wrote in a report.

De Cos reckons this time could be different from prior crashes because of greater consumer investments in stocks that could then hurt spending, more of a global focus on US equities, and the possibility of domestic asset bubbles caused by local AI-related export booms.

The dynamics of the current situation pose particular risks, he added, noting that AI investment is concentrating among only a few players, and capital spending outpaces cashflow at such companies, prompting them to rely on debt and private credit.
Moreover, a lot of that activity is “opaque and interconnected.”
“I do not say that this is where the AI boom must lead,” he said. “But the scale and speed of the current investment boom, and the weight of expected commercial returns, do warrant some caution.”
De Cos also cited the separate stability risk to cyber security, noting prior research that suggests AI could “tilt the balance in favor of attackers.”

A former Bank of Spain governor, de Cos is a possible successor to European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde. At a time of mounting speculation that she will resign from that job early, a publisher this month revealed her plans to publish memoirs in late January.

facts.text: LONDON, October 05, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--New research from FICO (NYSE: FICO), a leading global analytics software firm, shows that fraud leaders across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) are grappling with rising fraud complexity and AI-enabled threats, even as they accelerate investment in AI-driven detection and enterprise-wide fraud strategy.
And nearly half ranked effective AI integration as a top challenge, underscoring that embedding AI into existing fraud controls remains as much an operational hurdle as a technological one.
"Fraud in EMEA is not accelerating out of control, but it is becoming far more sophisticated, and that shift matters just as much," said Adam Davies, vice president, Product Management at FICO .

"Fraudsters now have access to the same generative and agentic AI tools that banks are deploying to stop them, and they are using them to scale social engineering, synthetic identities and deepfake-enabled attacks.

The institutions pulling ahead are the ones connecting their fraud functions across the enterprise and orchestrating every intelligence source they have, rather than adding point solutions one at a time."
Other highlights from the FICO research for EMEA:

Third-party vendor models now carry the greatest influence over EMEA fraud decisions (46%), far more than in-house models (24%), reflecting growing reliance on external expertise to keep pace with evolving threats

"The next 24 months will be defined by orchestration, not by any single piece of technology," Davies added.

Shane Riedman (pictured), president of anti-fraud analytics at the data analytics firm, told Insurance Business the convergence of widespread AI tools and shifting consumer attitudes, especially among the younger generations, has created a “perfect storm” for insurers.
This dynamic, he said, is already driving operational changes and could significantly impact policyholders.
Verisk found nearly all carriers surveyed (98%) said AI-powered tools are fueling a rise in digital fraud, and 76% reported that manipulated claims have become more sophisticated in the past year.

Despite heavy investment in AI-powered fraud detection, insurers are locked in a continuous battle with fraudsters.
The rise in AI-driven fraud is expected to have ripple effects across the insurance ecosystem, particularly for brokers and their clients.

Reuters reported on November 11 that the service was operational, following its September announcement of plans to enter the digital asset custody market. The offering covers Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), USD Coin (USDC), EURC and EURAU, with Deutsche Bank managing digital wallets and private keys on behalf of clients. Paul Maley, Deutsche Bank's global head of trust and securities services, said the bank intends to expand beyond custody into other blockchain-based financial services. “In the medium term we aim to deliver a fully integrated, regulated ecosystem that supports the custody, tokenisation, and settlement of digital assets,” Maley said. Deutsche Bank crypto custody service opens to institutional clients Deutsche Bank's September announcement outlined plans to provide custody services to institutional investors, asset managers, hedge funds, brokers, corporations and sovereign institutions. The service is now available to paying clients, although the bank has not publicly identified its first customers or disclosed the fees charged for holding digital assets. Under the arrangement, Deutsche Bank handles the technology needed to store and transfer cryptocurrencies, including the management of clients' private keys. Customers can access the platform through the bank's Autobahn corporate banking system. Its digital asset custody platform offers hardware-protected private key storage, warm and cold wallets, multiple approval controls and separate storage arrangements for client assets. The bank previously explained that its infrastructure would use external technology providers for selected technical services. Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate banking division, outlined the expansion plans in October, linking the initiative to growing institutional demand for digital assets and blockchain-based financial services. The planned rollout includes services for exchanging traditional currencies into stablecoins, tokenized deposits and support for issuing digital bonds. Podobnik previously said blockchain services would complement the bank's existing financial operations. The expansion forms part of Deutsche Bank's corporate banking growth strategy, which targets approximately 8% compound annual revenue growth between 2025 and 2028. On November 11, the lender announced a memorandum of understanding with Deutsche Asset Management, formerly known as DWS, to explore commercial and technical cooperation involving digital assets. Other financial institutions, including State Street, have developed digital asset custody infrastructure, while specialist providers such as BitGo and Anchorage Digital offer cryptocurrency custody services to institutional customers. Deutsche Bank's launch comes one day after reports that Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Banco Santander and Deutsche Bank were among financial institutions backing a new stablecoin venture with approximately $270 million in committed funding.

sources.title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
passages: Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million.
The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating.
By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians.
Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV.
PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care.
From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30.

extraction.body: Oura just made its biggest bet yet on AI-powered healthcare, announcing a $625 million acquisition of Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care startup. The deal comes just weeks after the smart ring maker postponed its $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing market uncertainty. The move signals a major strategic shift for Oura - from hardware maker to integrated health services platform - and represents one of the largest healthtech acquisitions of 2026. The Finnish smart ring maker announced today it's acquiring Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care startup, for $625 million in a mix of cash and stock. It's a bold move that transforms Oura from a hardware company into something much bigger - a vertically integrated health platform that combines biometric tracking with actual medical care. Just weeks ago, Oura postponed its planned IPO that could have valued the company at up to $2.2 billion. The company cited "uncertainty in the IPO market" as the reason for the delay. Now, instead of going public, Oura is doubling down on a strategy that could redefine what a wearables company can be. Counsel Health brings AI-powered primary care directly to patients, using machine learning models to triage symptoms, recommend treatments, and connect users with human physicians when needed. The startup's technology analyzes patient data in real-time, offering personalized health guidance that goes far beyond what a fitness tracker can provide. For Oura, which has built its reputation on sleep and recovery tracking through its signature ring, the acquisition opens a direct path to monetizing the health data it collects. The deal puts Oura in direct competition with tech giants circling the healthcare space. Apple has been steadily adding health features to the Apple Watch, while Amazon continues to expand its pharmacy and telehealth services. But Oura's approach is different - it's betting that combining passive biometric monitoring with AI-driven care can create a seamless health experience that neither pure hardware nor pure software companies can match. The $625 million price tag is significant, especially for a company that just pulled its IPO. It suggests Oura either has strong backing from existing investors or is confident enough in its cash position to make this bet. The company has raised over $300 million from investors including Dexcom, Eisai, and several high-profile individuals. Those backers are now betting on a very different company than the one they initially funded. This acquisition fits into a broader pattern of AI tools driving up healthcare costs, with Blue Cross Blue Shield data showing AI adoption led to nearly $1 billion in additional spending over two years. But Oura is betting it can flip that equation - using AI to make primary care more efficient and accessible, not more expensive. Even Healthcare recently hit a $300M valuation with backing from Khosla Ventures, while countless startups are racing to apply AI to everything from diagnostics to drug discovery. Counsel Health's acquisition suggests the consolidation phase is beginning, with established players like Oura buying technology rather than building it from scratch. For Oura's existing users, the acquisition could mean their sleep and activity data suddenly becomes far more actionable. The execution will depend on how well Oura can integrate Counsel Health's technology with its hardware and whether users are comfortable with that level of data sharing. The deal also raises questions about Oura's path to profitability. The company has been burning cash to grow its user base and develop new products. Adding a primary care service could create a recurring revenue stream through subscription fees or insurance partnerships, but it also adds complexity and regulatory burden. Healthcare is a notoriously difficult business, with thin margins and heavy compliance requirements. Oura's pivot mirrors moves by other wearables companies struggling to differentiate in a crowded market. Fitbit sold to Google for $2.1 billion in 2021. Whoop remains private but has raised hundreds of millions to build out its subscription model. The hardware alone isn't enough anymore - companies need services, data insights, and deeper integration into users' lives to justify their valuations. The acquisition comes at a time when privacy concerns are mounting around AI wearables, with regulators and consumers increasingly wary of how health data gets used. Oura will need to navigate those concerns carefully as it integrates Counsel Health's AI capabilities. Counsel Health's team and technology will be integrated into Oura's operations, though details on timing and how the service will be offered remain unclear. Will it be bundled with Oura's existing subscription?

coreStoryFacts.text: Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million.
The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating.
By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians.
Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV.
PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care.
From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30.
