sources.title: Cambridge Surveillance Technology Resident Assembly Weighs ShotSpotter, Security Cameras in Second Meeting - The Harvard Crimson
passages: Cambridge’s 40-person resident assembly on surveillance technology held its second meeting on Saturday — marking the halfway point before the body is set to deliver recommendations on surveillance and violence prevention efforts to the City Council.
But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department.
Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night.
The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence.
CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday.
But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents.
DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures.

The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly.
The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415.

extraction.body: Residents from across Cambridge gathered Saturday morning to help shape the city’s approach to public safety in the first-ever civic assembly held in Massachusetts. Among the group was a woman approaching her 80th birthday who has lived in the same building in The Port for half a century, three Cambridge Rindge and Latin School students, a mental health clinician who moved from Chicago nearly two decades ago, a third-generation Cantabrigian living in West Cambridge a woman who values Cambridge’s walkability but feels unsafe when walking home late at night and a lifelong North Cambridge resident concerned about recent shootings in her neighborhood. All are among the 40 residents selected by lottery to reflect Cambridge’s demographics, and had volunteered to participate (each will receive a $1,000 stipend for completing the four sessions). They will weigh the future of the city’s ShotSpotter gunshot detection system and surveillance cameras in public parks. And they may help heal a city riven by a death some think might have been prevented had the sound detection system not been deactivated by Cambridge’s City Council May 18. “When this process is finished, I hope you have done more than just make recommendations about technology,” said the Rev. Dr. Jeremy Battle, senior pastor of The Avenue Fellowship and a member of the assembly’s advisory committee, which helps guide the process, review educational materials and ensure participants hear balanced perspectives. “I hope you will have strengthened the way the city of Cambridge listens to itself from this inaugural moment.” The civic assembly was set in motion Aug. 3, when the council voted 6-3 to temporarily restore ShotSpotter and gather citizens to help determine its future. The assembly will meet for seven hours a session over four Saturdays through Dec. 5, then present recommendations to the City Council. The council is not obligated to adopt them. The first session can be viewed here . They started with data. Cambridge Police Department crime analysts Meghan LaMonica and Rebecca Leonard reviewed local crime trends showing the city recorded 475 violent crimes in 2025, less than half its 1990 peak of 1,077, although serious crime has risen since reaching a 55-year low in 2019. Gun violence remains concentrated in a handful of neighborhoods. Of 134 confirmed gunfire incidents citywide between January 2014 and Oct. 15, 2026, 68 occurred in The Port, and that neighborhood together with Cambridgeport and Wellington-Harrington, accounted for roughly 70% of incidents. ShotSpotter covers approximately 1.25 square miles, or 18%, of Cambridge’s land area, encompassing much of those neighborhoods. Although that area accounted for 74% of confirmed shootings between July 2014 and May 2026, ShotSpotter detected only 58 of the 96 confirmed shootings within its coverage area, a rate of 60%. Between 2015 and 2025, 35% of ShotSpotter alerts corresponded to confirmed shootings, compared with 18% of gunfire-related 911 calls. Following upgrades in 2021, ShotSpotter’s confirmation rate rose to 53% between 2022 and 2025. “Just because an alert is unfounded, it does not definitively mean that a shooting did not occur,” Leonard said. “It just means there was no evidence located that there had been a shooting.” Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them. In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes. A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024. Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared. “These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.” Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties. Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence. He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use. Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier. “My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.” Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system. Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge. She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest. “ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.” Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations. Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit. Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence. In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement. “I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.” As a nonprofit, community-based independent publication, we rely on contributions from readers like you to fund our journalism. On December 1, Cambridge residents can start renewing their resident parking permits, and for the first time since 2013, the price is going up, from $25 to $75. Though this may seem like a large increase, the true price was never really $25. Rather, neighbors without cars were paying part of the difference. “Just because an alert is unfounded, it does not definitively mean that a shooting did not occur,” Leonard said. “It just means there was no evidence located that there had been a shooting.”

Ermus St. Louis, an assistant professor at Northeastern University, presented research on surveillance technologies nationwide, urging participants to distinguish between technologies that help police respond to crimes and those that prevent them.

In Chicago, which discontinued ShotSpotter in September 2024, a 2021 inspector general investigation found that just 9.1% of police responses to more than 50,000 alerts produced documented evidence of a gun-related crime. A separate 2024 study found that ShotSpotter increased firearm recoveries by roughly 11% but did not significantly reduce shootings or other serious gun crimes.

A yearlong pilot in Durham, N.C., reduced median police response times by 1.2 minutes, but the system detected only 26 of 52 shootings involving injuries or deaths, compared with 50 reported through 911 calls. Researchers could not determine whether the technology reduced gun violence, and Durham declined to extend the program in March 2024.

Assembly members are also considering whether surveillance cameras should be in public parks. St. Louis pointed to programs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, noting that neither had demonstrated a reduction in crime. He urged participants to consider who would monitor Cambridge’s proposed cameras and how recordings would be stored and shared.
“These often try to solve relational problems with technology, right, and it’s just a quick fix,” St. Louis said. “It’s not going to address the underlying issues that’s causing problems.”

Following lunch, Gideon Epstein, policy counsel for the ACLU of Massachusetts’ Technology for Liberty program and a Cambridge resident, made the day’s first full-throated case for discontinuing ShotSpotter, arguing that it threatens residents’ privacy and civil liberties.

Epstein cited a 2015 Massachusetts Superior Court case, Commonwealth v. Denison , in which ShotSpotter recorded a conversation surrounding a fatal shooting. A judge ruled that the recording violated the state’s wiretap law and suppressed the evidence.

He also criticized Cambridge’s limited oversight of ShotSpotter, which was installed before the city adopted a 2018 ordinance requiring City Council approval before deploying new surveillance technologies. ShotSpotter’s approximately $50,000 annual cost is covered through a federal Department of Homeland Security grant administered by Boston, which holds the contract with ShotSpotter’s parent company, SoundThinking. The company owns the collected data, while Cambridge licenses its use.
Epstein questioned how the data could be shared without direct local control, noting that the ACLU had yet to receive information it requested from the city nearly three months earlier.

“My ask to this assembly is that you recommend that the city council discontinue ShotSpotter deployment,” Epstein said. “And to the extent residents believe that we need this kind of audio monitoring or gunshot detection technology, let’s start from square one. Let’s follow what the surveillance technology ordinance calls for, which is a public hearing, impact assessments, and a vote from the city council before any deployment happens.”

Assembly members also heard a defense of ShotSpotter from Cambridge Acting Police Commissioner Pauline Wells. She argues that while it cannot prevent shootings, it helps officers locate victims, provide emergency care and collect evidence. She urged participants to recommend keeping the system.

Wells emphasized that alerts do not automatically establish that a shooting occurred or make nearby residents suspects. She reported no civilian complaints or uses of force associated with ShotSpotter responses during its 12 years in Cambridge.

She cited a July 2024 shooting on Harvard Street in which she credited an early alert with saving a man’s life, a September 2022 alert that led police to recover a loaded handgun near the King Open School a few hours before students arrived, and an August 2022 alert that prompted a domestic violence investigation at Putnam Gardens, resulting in an arrest.

“ShotSpotter may not detect every shooting, but we’ve seen situations here in Cambridge where it has helped officers respond faster, [provide] life-saving care, and recover dangerous weapons,” Wells said. “Just because a tool doesn’t work 100% of the time doesn’t mean it isn’t valuable, especially when it has the potential to save someone’s life.”

Challenging Epstein’s privacy concerns, Wells said ShotSpotter’s sensors retain audio on a rolling 24-hour basis, overwriting it unless multiple sensors detect possible gunfire. Only short recordings associated with alerts are preserved. However, a recording she played of an actual Cambridge shooting included audible human voices, which she acknowledged while maintaining that the system was not designed to monitor conversations.
Wells also defended the federal funding arrangement, arguing that ShotSpotter’s lack of direct cost to Cambridge was a benefit.

Following the presentations, participants broke into smaller groups before reconvening to share principles they believed should guide Cambridge’s use of surveillance technology. Several emphasized local control over surveillance data, transparency and regular evaluations of effectiveness. One group argued that Cambridge should control data collected within its borders, while another called for safeguards to track who accesses sensitive information. Others stressed that technology should complement, rather than replace, community relationships and efforts to address the causes of violence.
In a statement Monday, Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, who attended the morning portion of the assembly, praised participants’ thoughtful questions and engagement.

“I also want them to know that their work matters,” Siddiqui said. “The City Council called for this assembly, and we have a responsibility to take their recommendations seriously and explain how they inform our decisions.”

CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday.
But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents.
DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures.

extraction.body: Cambridge’s 40-person resident assembly on surveillance technology held its second meeting on Saturday — marking the halfway point before the body is set to deliver recommendations on surveillance and violence prevention efforts to the City Council. Saturday’s meeting centered on outlining issues with existing surveillance technology — and the city’s broader response to residents’ concerns. The assembly was created as a response to concerns that the City Council had failed to listen to residents as it wavered over the future of ShotSpotter, the automatic gunshot detection system. The City Council voted to remove the technology in May, citing privacy concerns, and reversed the decision in August after the fatal shooting of 32-year-old Xavier Bautista, a Public Works Department employee. The Council’s order to reinstate ShotSpotter, a network of microphones that detect loud noises and alert police of potential gunfire, was a temporary move, delaying a further decision until the end of the resident assembly. The assembly has so far hosted a slate of speakers — including activists, surveillance technology researchers, city officials, and family members of people who have been impacted by gun violence. The Black Response, an activist group that has spent years pushing the city to end its use of ShotSpotter presented at Saturday’s meeting. “What kind of city do we want to live in?” Virginia Cuello, a member of The Black Response asked “One that pays for microphones and sends multiple officers to a loud noise, or one that invests in the people and services that keep us safe?” But much of Saturday’s meeting focused on another surveillance effort: increasing security cameras operated by the Cambridge Police Department. CPD shared three draft proposals for expanding security cameras in public parks on Saturday. All three options included scaling the number of cameras based on the number of calls CPD has received at each location over the last two years. Pigeon Park received the most calls for service during the period, 370, followed by Danehy Park with 171. Russell Field saw 148, and Cambridge Common saw 139. The first proposal would have added ten cameras across the city for roughly $118,276, while the second proposal would have added 15 cameras for about $177,415. The final proposal came at the highest price tag, suggesting an additional twenty-five cameras would cost more than $295,692. Under each proposal, the funding would come partially from a Department of Homeland Security Urban Area Security Initiative grant. Fatuma Hussein, a member of the assembly, said she supported the expansion of security cameras, as they make her feel safer when walking in Cambridge at night. “I like to walk sometimes at night, so when I go to the Charles River, they have a camera there, and I feel safe because I know there’s a camera,” Hussein said. But some members expressed skepticism about the proposed camera installations, questioning the need for increased surveillance of residents. Troy A. DaCosta, an assembly member, said cameras are “a tool,” but raised concerns over preferring them over alternative measures. “How are we going to implement these properly? Whether it’s like having better surveillance with people, like monitoring the parks, as in like visiting the parks, better lighting, or better community engagement,” DaCosta said. The assembly is slated to convene two more times over the next month, to outline its priorities and draft recommendations to the City Council in early December. —Staff writer Shawn A. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Investors who favor Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) clearly prioritize growth. SpaceX soared into the stock market spotlight with its debut in June, the biggest initial public offering on record. Raising more than $85 billion and immediately joining the trillion-dollar club, SpaceX easily captured the attention of investors. The stock, however, hasn't performed as those investors may have expected: It's declined 16% since it started trading. While investors like SpaceX's growth, they may be less pleased with the company's capital expenditures. In the recent quarter, capex came in at more than $19 billion, surpassing the company's $14 billion in revenue. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » If you're looking for growth, should you forget SpaceX and buy the following two artificial intelligence (AI) stocks instead? Let's find out. When you think of top AI chips, you may think of market leader Nvidia . But another company is also delivering enormous growth in this area. I'm talking about Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD). For years, this player has been a leader in the central processing unit (CPU) market -- these are the chips found in all computers -- but entered the AI chip market later than Nvidia. Today, however, AMD is catching up nicely. The company has reported growth quarter after quarter, thanks to its progress in the area of graphics processing units (GPUs), or the chips that power key AI tasks. AMD confirmed this in the recent period, with record sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs. And total data center revenue surged 97% to a record $8.5 billion. This may look slim compared to Nvidia's $89 billion in data center sales, but considering AMD's commitment to AI chip development, I see this as an opportunity. AMD may find it easier from these levels to deliver tremendous growth than a company that already has the revenue levels of Nvidia. extraction.body: Broadcom and Applied Digital could be smarter AI infrastructure plays right now. Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom ( AVGO +3.91% ) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia 's graphics processing units ( GPUs) , while Applied Digital ( APLD -0.24% ) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look. Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure . Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads. The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet , Meta Platforms , and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips. That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter. The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years. But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom. Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation. But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture. Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads. It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion. Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. Its Polaris Forge 1 campus in North Dakota has already kicked off operations, and additional capacity will keep coming online as construction continues. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities. Another important development was its move to hive off its cloud services business into a new public company, ChronoScale ( CHRN -7.14% ) . This will allow Applied Digital to focus more on developing and running large-scale AI campuses. That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models. Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology. For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks. Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote . “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote . “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. sources.title: OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
passages: With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at.
It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to make ChatGPT a direct e-commerce hub.
However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company retired the effort , which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.

On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the kind of profiles that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services.
Benji Shomair, OpenAI’s VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”
Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.

“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”

sources.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
passages: Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to the Apple Watch and Android’s Wear OS, the company announced on Monday.
With the launch, users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation directly on their smartwatch.
A few days ago, Meta launched Spaces , a new way to communicate and collaborate with Muse.
Spaces function as dedicated conversations around specific topics, which Meta describes as “custom experiences” as they’re mini apps that are built on the fly.
They appear in the sidebar of the Muse interface and bring up a focused conversation where the AI agent works toward a particular goal on the user’s behalf.
Last week, Meta rolled out the ability for users in the U.S. to video chat with their Muse AI avatar.
Meta said Muse will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that reflect the tone and context of the conversation as it speaks.
It’s worth noting that Muse doesn’t actually see users, but can hear them and respond in real time.
Works around the clock, and now on your wrist.
The smartwatch launch comes just a month after Meta introduced a dedicated iPad app for Muse.
Despite being a relatively new product, Meta has wasted little time introducing new capabilities to Muse.
Muse is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents competing for users’ attention.

Like many of its competitors, it allows users to connect their accounts to manage email, meetings, bills, and more, while also handling tasks such as booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.
Users can also personalize their Muse avatar to their liking and change it into something that resembles a person, an animal, or another type of character.

sources.title: Proximal Ventures raises debut fund to back startups bringing AI to drug development
passages: Raoof’s firm, Proximal Ventures , is betting that AI can transform the tools, infrastructure, and services that support drug development.
Proximal plans to invest in pre-seed and seed-stage startups, writing checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million.

The firm has already backed seven startups, including ChronicleBio, co-founded by former OpenAI executive Fidji Simo, which uses AI to analyze biological and medical data to better understand chronic diseases and identify potential treatments.
While established venture firms continue to attract capital, first-time fund managers are facing one of the toughest fundraising environments in years.
But that didn’t stop Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor and executive at two healthcare startups, from raising $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund.
It is these qualities that have helped Proximal invest in startups alongside some of the better-known, much larger funds, she added.
Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch.

extraction.body: While established venture firms continue to attract capital, first-time fund managers are facing one of the toughest fundraising environments in years. But that didn’t stop Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor and executive at two healthcare startups, from raising $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund. Raoof’s firm, Proximal Ventures , is betting that AI can transform the tools, infrastructure, and services that support drug development. Pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced various stages of drug development to specialized service providers, from synthesizing thousands of molecular compounds and figuring out how to manufacture drugs at scale to analyzing clinical trial data. “For a long time, the assumption was that pharma is not a great buyer of software, but a really good buyer of services,” Raoof told TechCrunch. Raoof believes AI could automate much of that work, creating an opportunity for startups to capture billions of dollars in pharmaceutical industry spending. By using AI, these companies could deliver the same services at a lower cost and in significantly less time, he said. Some of the most valuable applications of AI so far have been in service-oriented industries like law and finance, Raoof said. He sees similar opportunities in pharmaceutical services. Proximal plans to invest in pre-seed and seed-stage startups, writing checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million. The firm has already backed seven startups, including ChronicleBio, co-founded by former OpenAI executive Fidji Simo, which uses AI to analyze biological and medical data to better understand chronic diseases and identify potential treatments. Before spending two years as a principal at SignalFire, Raoof led business development at clinical trial recruitment startup Iterative Health and previously oversaw partnerships at Flatiron Health, an oncology data company acquired by Roche for $1.9 billion in 2018. “If you’re building a company that’s selling into the life sciences, one of the hardest things to do is starting that initial commercial flywheel,” Raoof said. His sales chops, deep understanding of the healthcare ecosystem, and extensive industry relationships gave limited partners, the investors in VC funds, the confidence that he could spot strong startups and help them land customers. Proximal’s backers include VC firms SignalFire and Kleiner Perkins, Bertelsmann Healthcare Investments, and individual investors such as Dimension Capital co-founders Nan Li and Zavain Dar. Amy Abernethy, co-founder of Highlander Health and former principal deputy commissioner of the FDA, is also an investor. She first met Raoof when they worked together at Flatiron Health, where she served as chief medical officer. She told TechCrunch that his ability to build relationships and spot industry bottlenecks made a lasting impression. Abernethy is convinced that his abilities, along with the understanding of what the healthcare market needs, will make him a successful investor. It is these qualities that have helped Proximal invest in startups alongside some of the better-known, much larger funds, she added. “If you’re building a company that’s selling into the life sciences, one of the hardest things to do is starting that initial commercial flywheel,” Raoof said.

extraction.body: Adobe will open its Creative Cloud applications to third-party AI assistants, with the ability to edit content in Photoshop, After Effects, Illustrator, and Premiere from tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, the company announced at its Max event. The model context protocol (MCP) integration, due in private beta in early 2027, would let third-party AI assistants to make changes to content in Creative Cloud desktop applications, without losing the ability to adjust individual elements of a design or video manually afterwards. For example, a third-party AI assistant could remove a logo from multiple advertising campaign assets. “Make the change once, then ask your agent to cascade it across the rest of the campaign, and step in at any moment to refine the work by hand,” said Deepa Subramaniam, Adobe’s VP, product marketing for Creative Cloud, in a blog post Tuesday. Third-party agents could also connect to other apps in a single workflow, so it would be possible to “pull in a project brief from Google Docs, work on it in Adobe’s tools and share the result with your team via Slack,” for example, Subramaniam said. The MCP connections can help creative professionals “keep their work where they choose to work, without sacrificing the upside of modern collaborative and secure systems,” said Liz Miller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research. For them, these connections are another tool that opens up access to so much more of their toolkit.” Keith Kirkpatrick, vice president of research at The Futurum Group, also anticipates demand from Adobe users to access Creative Cloud apps via third-party AI assistants, though he expects it will appeal most to a “fairly specific crowd” of “creative technologists, production teams, and power users who already spend their day in Claude or ChatGPT and want an agent to take care of the tedious stuff: organizing assets, setting up layers, building out sequences.” “Most creative pros are still going to want their hands in the application,” he said. Opening access to Creative Cloud apps via third-party agents could potentially loosen the direct relationship Adobe has with customers — a scenario that many software vendors are now grappling with. For Adobe, it’s a necessary adaptation, as employees increase their use of AI assistants to get work done. “Companies are using several AI models at once, and people are starting more of their work inside these assistants,” said Kirkpatrick. “If that’s where the request starts, Adobe wants to be the one doing the work behind it.” Gartner predicts that enterprise AI assistants will account for more of knowledge workers’ daily interaction time than any other application within the next three years, according to a recent Magic Quadrant report. Miller said that opening its applications to third-party tools could be beneficial for Adobe’s business. “This won't negatively impact Adobe's place with their core creative, marketing, or business users,” she said. “For users who have found their flow and patterns of work in ChatGPT or Claude, [they can] stay there but still access the skills and tools you need to use to generate the quality of work expected,” Miller said. The MCP integration in Creative Cloud is the latest part of Adobe’s strategy to embrace third-party AI assistants — Adobe has previously announced ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini integrations that provide limited editing capabilities for apps such as Acrobat, Photoshop, Premiere, Express, and Lightroom, directly within the AI assistants. This contrasts with the new MCP integrations that let AI assistants make changes directly to content in Adobe’s desktop applications. “The real question is whether any of this turns into paying Adobe customers, and Adobe hasn’t shown that yet with its existing connectors,” said Kirkpatrick. “Adobe’s edge has to be that its tools are better and that it comes with the IP and brand controls enterprises need.” Firefly upgrades — Builder, Design, and ‘always-on’ agents The MCP integration was one of numerous agent-related announcements at Adobe Max on Tuesday, with other updates aimed at enhancing native functionality within Creative Cloud and the Firefly AI assistant. This includes “always-on” agents that work in the background, taking on recurring tasks for users. Users choose from pre-built agents aimed at specific workflows, then customize what actions the agent takes, set goals, and review plans before it begins. The agents ask for approval for certain decisions, learn preferences from feedback, and are managed via a central dashboard in Firefly. “On a multi-week video project, for example, an always-on agent can organize incoming footage, remove duplicate clips, and flag camera shake or audio issues for your review,” Mike Polner, vice president of product marketing, Creators at Adobe, said in a blog post. “For the right person, I think it’s an easy sell,” said Kirkpatrick, such as a social media manager starting their day with a batch of draft posts to review, though it may be less appealing to creative professionals responsible for generating broader ideas. For some end users, the always-on agents can be “an additional set of hands to drive efficiency,” said Miller, while “others will see this as a force multiplier, allowing them to expand their business flow … while the assistant handles the sorting and cleaning.” Customers who use the always-on agent should ensure there are sufficient guardrails in place, said Kirkpatrick. “Before activating an always-on agent, I’d want to know exactly what it can touch, and I’d make sure it drafts but never publishes on its own. Everything it makes should get a brand check,” he said. He cited Adobe’s own survey of marketing and creative professionals that showed that around a believe that public-facing content is “off-brand.” “An agent working around the clock can make that a lot worse if nobody’s paying attention,” said Kirkpatrick. Managing costs of an always-on agent with budget controls is another consideration, he said. Adobe hasn’t disclosed full pricing information at this stage. Always-on agents, launching in beta in early 2027, will initially be available for Adobe Firefly. Other Firefly capabilities announced at the MAX event include Firefly Builder, in private beta, which creates prototypes of websites and interactive apps from natural language prompts. While Adobe builds out its own native and third-party AI features, it also faces competition from other software tools aimed at creative professionals. “From a competitive perspective, I see Canva and Figma going after the same in-house teams and are showing up in the same AI assistants,” said Kirkpatrick. Adobe also faces competition from AI model providers such as Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that are building design tools into their products. “Where Adobe really wins is when precision, brand control and commercially safe content matter, and that’s mostly in the enterprise,” said Kirkpatrick. “With individual creators, its lead is a lot smaller, and where Adobe is most at risk for displacement.”

“Before activating an always-on agent, I’d want to know exactly what it can touch, and I’d make sure it drafts but never publishes on its own.
Everything it makes should get a brand check,” he said.

He cited Adobe’s own survey of marketing and creative professionals that showed that around a believe that public-facing content is “off-brand.” “An agent working around the clock can make that a lot worse if nobody’s paying attention,” said Kirkpatrick.

Always-on agents, launching in beta in early 2027, will initially be available for Adobe Firefly.

“For the right person, I think it’s an easy sell,” said Kirkpatrick, such as a social media manager starting their day with a batch of draft posts to review, though it may be less appealing to creative professionals responsible for generating broader ideas.

“Before activating an always-on agent, I’d want to know exactly what it can touch, and I’d make sure it drafts but never publishes on its own.
Everything it makes should get a brand check,” he said.

He cited Adobe’s own survey of marketing and creative professionals that showed that around a believe that public-facing content is “off-brand.” “An agent working around the clock can make that a lot worse if nobody’s paying attention,” said Kirkpatrick.

Adobe hasn’t disclosed full pricing information at this stage.

While Adobe builds out its own native and third-party AI features, it also faces competition from other software tools aimed at creative professionals.
“From a competitive perspective, I see Canva and Figma going after the same in-house teams and are showing up in the same AI assistants,” said Kirkpatrick.
Adobe also faces competition from AI model providers such as Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that are building design tools into their products.
“Where Adobe really wins is when precision, brand control and commercially safe content matter, and that’s mostly in the enterprise,” said Kirkpatrick.
“With individual creators, its lead is a lot smaller, and where Adobe is most at risk for displacement.”

sources.title: Pixel Tag, Google’s $30 Android-ready answer to Apple’s AirTag, is now available
passages: Google’s answer to Apple’s AirTag, the Google Pixel Tag , goes on sale starting Tuesday, allowing Android users to track items like their keys, wallet, or bag using their smartphone’s built-in Find Hub.
Google didn’t originally say that the Pixel Tag included NFC when it announced the device in August.
Google uses the tap gesture to instead connect the user to the device’s settings.

The network, similar to competitive offerings from Apple and Tile, taps into the connectivity provided by other Android devices, which can identify and share the location of the lost item back to its owner.
This location information is displayed on a map inside the Find Hub app.
The slimness of the device might make it more appealing for some, particularly if they’re adding the tag to a small item, like a keychain.
First announced in August , the $29.99 device takes cues from the AirTag and other lost-item finders by offering connectivity via Bluetooth and ultra-wideband for precision finding.
This lets Android device owners, including Pixel Watch wearers, locate their missing items using a combination of visual distance and directional guidance.

While the person who found the item can’t tap it, as with NFC-enabled devices, Pixel Tags that are put into “Lost” mode will be able to share the owner’s email, number, and a short message so the person who finds the tag can contact you.
Meanwhile, the device itself is made from stainless steel and features IP67 water and dust resistance (maximum depth of 1 meter up to 30 minutes).
It pairs with devices running Android 9 or newer via Fast Pair technology.

extraction.body: Google’s answer to Apple’s AirTag, the Google Pixel Tag , goes on sale starting Tuesday, allowing Android users to track items like their keys, wallet, or bag using their smartphone’s built-in Find Hub. First announced in August , the $29.99 device takes cues from the AirTag and other lost-item finders by offering connectivity via Bluetooth and ultra-wideband for precision finding. This lets Android device owners, including Pixel Watch wearers, locate their missing items using a combination of visual distance and directional guidance. Plus, the tag has a built-in speaker to play a chime that helps you locate your item if nearby. (Or, if you’ve lost your phone, you can press the button on the Pixel Tag twice to ring it, too.) You can choose between three different levels of loudness in the settings within the Find Hub, with the maximum volume around 80 decibels. Though the Pixel Tag serves the same purpose as an AirTag, Google has opted for a different design. Instead of a small, round device, like Apple’s, the Pixel Tag is slimmer and more elongated. Spec-by-spec, the Pixel Tag is 1.1-inches wide, compared to the AirTag’s 1.26 inches. As the Pixel Tag is oval-shaped, it’s 1.8-inches high from top to bottom. Thickness-wise, the Pixel Tag clocks in at a depth of 0.2 inches, compared with the AirTag’s 0.31 inches (which Apple calls its height). The slimness of the device might make it more appealing for some, particularly if they’re adding the tag to a small item, like a keychain. The device weighs just 0.4 oz, with the battery included. Unlike Apple, Google opted for a physical button you can press on the tag, which makes it more obvious how it’s meant to work. Google didn’t originally say that the Pixel Tag included NFC when it announced the device in August. NFC is used by Apple’s AirTag to aid people who find lost items, as they can tap the side of the tag to launch a webpage that displays the owner’s contact information. Google uses the tap gesture to instead connect the user to the device’s settings. Meanwhile, for lost items that are not nearby, the Pixel Tag relies on Google’s crowdsourced network of over a billion Android devices globally. The network, similar to competitive offerings from Apple and Tile, taps into the connectivity provided by other Android devices, which can identify and share the location of the lost item back to its owner. This location information is displayed on a map inside the Find Hub app. While the person who found the item can’t tap it, as with NFC-enabled devices, Pixel Tags that are put into “Lost” mode will be able to share the owner’s email, number, and a short message so the person who finds the tag can contact you. When the tag comes back into range of the user’s phone, the item is automatically marked as found. The Pixel Tag’s location can also be shared with up to 10 people in the Find Hub app, which could be useful for shared items like the family car keys, which multiple people might rely on. Like AirTag, the Pixel Tag is powered by a user-replaceable coin cell battery (the CR2032), which makes the device reusable for the long term. (Google claims the device has up to one year of battery life to start.) Meanwhile, the device itself is made from stainless steel and features IP67 water and dust resistance (maximum depth of 1 meter up to 30 minutes). It pairs with devices running Android 9 or newer via Fast Pair technology. The Pixel Tag comes in two shades: silver and a pale green, and can be bought individually or in a four-pack for $99.99. Alongside the launch, the company Bellroy is debuting its own keychain cases in a variety of colors and styles, which will also be sold on the Google Store. Post updated after publication to note that the Pixel Tag now supports NFC, which was a surprise addition not mentioned at the time of its announcement. passages: Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking.
The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets.
When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck.
Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so the board builds while people talk, Anthropic says.

The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google.
Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks.
Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans.
At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow.
The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says.
With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant.
Anthropic also announced that Claude Data, formerly known as Claude Dashboards, is now generally available.
The feature connects Claude to systems that companies use to keep their numbers, like a data warehouse or CRM.
Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos.
Anthropic says Claude handles the initial setup of trackers and budgets, while allowing teams to continue refining and updating the same spreadsheet.
Each spreadsheet can include multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus.
Claude also makes edits directly in cells alongside the team, and outlines each change so users can see what it did.

Anthropic notes that teams can now open these apps directly alongside their Claude conversations and ask the assistant to work within them, essentially bringing existing workflows into the same workspace.

sources.title: Nvidia has a Jensen Huang problem—and no obvious successor
passages: The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company.
“If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position.
“Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.”

Huang’s total compensation last year of $36.3 million, of which the vast majority came in the form of stock awards, included some $4 million for security paid for by Nvidia, which filings say is “due to the exceptionally high public profile and prominence of our CEO.”
The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry.
Huang, who has cultivated an air of infallibility inside Nvidia, has given no indication he will step down from the role of CEO.
Despite his imperial stature, Huang owns just 3.6 percent of Nvidia.
That stake makes him Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder and is worth more than $150 billion.

However, Huang lacks the special voting rights held by many Silicon Valley founders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, that would allow him to control the board or face down outside investors who might attempt to oust him.

Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter who serves as a senior director in Nvidia’s product marketing team and has become an increasingly visible presence at the company’s conferences, canceled a planned appearance at a company event in South Korea on Monday.
Huang faces a board probe as investors fret over Nvidia’s lack of a clear successor.
“Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post.
These costs included protection at home and during “personal travel,” as well as using private aircraft for all business trips, according to filings.

The board’s public statement on Sunday said it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team” and that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend.
Huang leads a small core executive team at Nvidia, including Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, Operations Chief Debora Shoquist and general counsel Tim Teter.
A 2025 report by law firm Fenwick found that only one company in S&P 100—which would be Nvidia, according to its own filings—had no chair.

Jay Puri, a close lieutenant who led Nvidia’s sales operations and deputized for Huang on international visits, stepped down in August and was replaced on the executive team by Microsoft veteran Nick Parker.

Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine , portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership.
In its proxy filings, Nvidia states that this set-up “ensures that each member has an equal voice in the affairs and management of Nvidia.”
The law in Delaware, where Nvidia is incorporated, says executives have certain fiduciary duties including a duty of care and loyalty to their company.
Nvidia’s code of conduct requires executives to “conduct themselves with the highest degree of integrity, ethics and honesty.
Our credibility and reputation depend upon their good judgment, ethical standards and personal integrity.”

The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company. Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy. The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 percent by midday trading on Monday. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post. Nvidia’s chips were instrumental in the creation of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and now sit at the center of Big Tech’s $1 trillion AI infrastructure frenzy. Huang has personally stood behind investments and guarantees running into hundreds of billions of dollars for dozens of AI start-ups and data center providers, as well as lobbying US President Donald Trump for looser AI regulation. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” analysts at Bernstein said in a note to clients. With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend. The investigation will probably be led by board member and former Cooley chief executive Stephen C. Neal, according to people familiar with the probe. “If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position. “Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.” In contrast to other leading Big Tech companies, Nvidia’s annual reports and corporate governance paperwork make no specific reference to “succession planning” and set out no details for how it would replace its CEO, even in an emergency, beyond noting that the company “believe[s] in extensive leadership development.” Huang’s unusually large number of direct reports, numbered at more than 60 according to a 2024 disclosure, present Nvidia’s board with a “pool of excellent candidates for future promotion,” recent filings say. Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine , portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership. He is known to be able to inspire extraordinary productivity inside a company whose 42,000 employees each generated an average of more than $7 million in annual revenue over the past 12 months, far more than any other Big Tech group. But Kim also notes that Huang represents the company’s “single point of failure,” functioning as its head of marketing, sales, and product development. His influence in the wider tech industry is also unique. Endorsements by Huang of companies in the AI semiconductor supply chain can supercharge their share prices, while his offhand dismissal early last year of the near-term commercial prospects for quantum computing sent stocks in the sector spiraling. Despite his imperial stature, Huang owns just 3.6 percent of Nvidia. That stake makes him Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder and is worth more than $150 billion. Huang reimburses Nvidia for personal air travel on private aircraft arranged by the company, according to filings. Nvidia’s board, whose individual members have until now kept a low profile, confirmed they would appoint a special committee composed of sitting board members assisted by outside counsel to examine the allegations surrounding its CEO. Neal joined Nvidia’s board in 2019 and is chair emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, after serving as the law firm’s CEO from 2001 to 2008.
